308|_**Tyrannosaurus**_ ([/t ɪ ˌ r æ n ə ˈ s ɔː r ə s,t aɪ-/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"))[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-title-1) is a [genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genus "Genus") of large [theropod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theropoda "Theropoda") dinosaur. The [type species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_species "Type species")_**Tyrannosaurus rex**_ (_rex_ meaning 'king' in [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin")), often shortened to _**T. rex**_ or colloquially **T-Rex**, is one of the best represented theropods. It lived throughout what is now western [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), on what was then an island continent known as [Laramidia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laramidia "Laramidia"). _Tyrannosaurus_ had a much wider range than other [tyrannosaurids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosauridae "Tyrannosauridae"). [Fossils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil "Fossil") are found in a variety of [geological formations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geological_formations "Geological formations") which have been [dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geochronology "Geochronology") to the late [Maastrichtian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastrichtian "Maastrichtian") age of the late [Cretaceous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous "Cretaceous") period, 69 to 66[million years ago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mya_(unit) "Mya (unit)"), with isolated specimens possibly indicating an earlier origin in the middle [Campanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campanian "Campanian") age. It was one of the last known members of the tyrannosaurids and among the last non-[avian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird "Bird") dinosaurs to exist before the [Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous%E2%80%93Paleogene_extinction_event "Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event").
309|
310|Like other tyrannosaurids, _Tyrannosaurus_ was a [bipedal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biped "Biped") carnivore with a massive skull balanced by a long, heavy tail. Relative to its large and powerful hind limbs, the forelimbs of _Tyrannosaurus_ were short but unusually powerful for their size, and they had two clawed digits. The most complete specimen measures 12.3–12.4 m (40–41 ft) in length, but according to most modern estimates, _Tyrannosaurus_ could have exceeded sizes of 13 m (43 ft) in length, 3.7–4 m (12–13 ft) in hip height, and 8.8 t (8.7 long tons; 9.7 short tons) in mass. Although some other theropods might have rivaled or exceeded _Tyrannosaurus_ in [size](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur_size "Dinosaur size"), it is still among the largest known land predators, with its estimated bite force being the largest among all terrestrial animals. By far the largest carnivore in its environment, _Tyrannosaurus rex_ was most likely an [apex predator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apex_predator "Apex predator"), preying upon [hadrosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrosaur "Hadrosaur"), juvenile armored herbivores like [ceratopsians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceratopsia "Ceratopsia") and [ankylosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankylosaur "Ankylosaur"), and possibly [sauropods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauropod "Sauropod"). The question of whether _Tyrannosaurus_ was an apex predator or a pure scavenger was among the longest debates in [paleontology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleontology "Paleontology"). Most paleontologists today accept that _Tyrannosaurus_ was both a predator and a scavenger, and the idea of _Tyrannosaurus_ being primarily a scavenger has been discredited.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-2)
311|
312|Some [specimens of _Tyrannosaurus rex_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specimens_of_Tyrannosaurus "Specimens of Tyrannosaurus") are nearly complete skeletons. [Soft tissue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_tissue "Soft tissue") and [proteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein "Protein") have been reported in at least one of these specimens. The abundance of fossil material has allowed significant research into many aspects of the animal's biology, including its life history and [biomechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomechanics "Biomechanics"). The feeding habits, [physiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology"), and potential speed of _Tyrannosaurus rex_ are a few subjects of debate. Its [taxonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxonomy_(biology) "Taxonomy (biology)") is also controversial. The Asian _[Tarbosaurus bataar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarbosaurus\_bataar "Tarbosaurus bataar")_ is very closely related to _Tyrannosaurus_ and has sometimes been seen as a species of this genus. Several North American tyrannosaurids have been [synonymized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synonym_(biology) "Synonym (biology)") with _Tyrannosaurus_, while some _Tyrannosaurus_ specimens have been proposed as distinct species. The validity of these species, such as the more recently discovered _**T. mcraeensis**_, is contentious.
313|
314|_Tyrannosaurus_ has been one of the best-known dinosaurs since the early 20th century. Science writer [Riley Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riley_Black "Riley Black") has called it the "ultimate dinosaur". Its fossils have been a popular attraction in museums and it has appeared in media like _[Jurassic Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurassic\_Park "Jurassic Park")_.

326|A tooth from what is now documented as a _Tyrannosaurus rex_ was found in July 1874 upon [South Table Mountain (Colorado)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Table_Mountain_(Colorado) "South Table Mountain (Colorado)") by [Jarvis Hall (Colorado)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarvis_Hall_(Colorado) "Jarvis Hall (Colorado)") student Peter T. Dotson under the auspices of [Arthur Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Lakes "Arthur Lakes") near [Golden, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden,_Colorado "Golden, Colorado"), in sediments belonging to the [Denver Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Formation "Denver Formation").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-3)_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite\_note-:02-4)_ In the early 1890s, [John Bell Hatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bell_Hatcher "John Bell Hatcher") collected postcranial elements in eastern [Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming "Wyoming"). The fossils were believed to be from the large species _[Ornithomimus grandis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornithomimus "Ornithomimus")_ (now _[Deinodon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinodon "Deinodon")_) but are now considered _T. rex_ remains.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-quinlanetal2007-5)
327|
328|In 1892, [Edward Drinker Cope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Drinker_Cope "Edward Drinker Cope") found two vertebral fragments of a large dinosaur. Cope believed the fragments belonged to an "agathaumid" ([ceratopsid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceratopsidae "Ceratopsidae")) dinosaur, and named them _Manospondylus gigas_, meaning "giant porous vertebra", in reference to the numerous openings for blood vessels he found in the bone.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-quinlanetal2007-5) The _M. gigas_ remains were, in 1907, identified by Hatcher as those of a theropod rather than a ceratopsid.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-6)
329|
330|[Henry Fairfield Osborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Fairfield_Osborn "Henry Fairfield Osborn") recognized the similarity between _Manospondylus gigas_ and _T. rex_ as early as 1917, by which time the second vertebra had been lost. Owing to the fragmentary nature of the _Manospondylus_ vertebrae, Osborn did not synonymize the two genera, instead considering the older genus indeterminate.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-osborn1917-7) In June 2000, the [Black Hills Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute "Black Hills Institute") found around 10% of a _Tyrannosaurus_ skeleton ([BHI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute "Black Hills Institute") 6248) at a site that might have been the original _M. gigas_ locality.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-larson2008-8) While Larson initially considered this specimen as the same animal as the _M. gigas_ holotype and suggested that it would take priority over _T. rex_, other researchers including Christopher Brochu remained skeptical that the name _T. rex_ would be abandoned.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-McTavish2000-9) In 2003, Brochu further argued that although both taxa probably represent the same species, it is impossible to demonstrate that the specimen discovered by the Black Hills Institute represents the same animal as _M. gigas_ due to the poor preservation of the _M. gigas_ holotype; additionally, following the 2000 [International Code of Zoological Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Code_of_Zoological_Nomenclature "International Code of Zoological Nomenclature") amendment, a name in popular usage like _T. rex_ has priority over a name with technical priority but not used as a valid name in formal literature after the year 1899 for over fifty years like _M. gigas_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wi... 332|### Skeleton discovery and naming
333|
334|[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Tyrannosaurus_skeleton.jpg/250px-Tyrannosaurus_skeleton.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_skeleton.jpg)
335|
336|Outdated skeletal restoration by [William D. Matthew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Diller_Matthew "William Diller Matthew") from 1905, published alongside Osborn's description paper
337|
338|[Barnum Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnum_Brown "Barnum Brown"), assistant curator of the [American Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Museum_of_Natural_History "American Museum of Natural History"), found the first partial skeleton of _T. rex_ in eastern Wyoming in 1900. Brown found another partial skeleton in the [Hell Creek Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell_Creek_Formation "Hell Creek Formation") in Montana in 1902, comprising approximately 34 fossilized bones.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-osborn1905-12) Writing at the time Brown said "Quarry No. 1 contains the femur, pubes, humerus, three vertebrae and two undetermined bones of a large Carnivorous Dinosaur not described by [Marsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Othniel_Charles_Marsh "Othniel Charles Marsh").... I have never seen anything like it from the [Cretaceous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous "Cretaceous")."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-dingus2010-13)[Henry Fairfield Osborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Fairfield_Osborn "Henry Fairfield Osborn"), president of the [American Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Museum_of_Natural_History "American Museum of Natural History"), named the second skeleton _T. rex_ in 1905. The generic name is derived from the [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language") words τύραννος (_tyrannos_, meaning "tyrant") and [σαῦρος](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%CF%83%CE%B1%E1%BF%A6%CF%81%CE%BF%CF%82 "wikt:σαῦρος") (_sauros_, meaning "lizard"). Osborn used the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language") word _rex_, meaning "king", for the specific name. The full [binomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_nomenclature "Binomial nomenclature") therefore translates to "tyrant lizard the king" or "King Tyrant Lizard", emphasizing the animal's size and presumed dominance o... [truncated]
339|
340|[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Dynamosaurus_holotype.jpg/250px-Dynamosaurus_holotype.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dynamosaurus_holotype.jpg)
341|
342|_Dynamosaurus imperiosus_[holotype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holotype "Holotype") (NHMUK PV R8020, previously AMNH 5886) on display at the [Natural History Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_History_Museum,_London "Natural History Museum, London"), London
343|
344|Osborn named the other specimen _Dynamosaurus imperiosus_ in a paper in 1905.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-osborn1905-12) In 1906, Osborn recognized that the two skeletons were from the same species and selected _Tyrannosaurus_ as the preferred name.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-osborn1906-14) In 1941, the _T. rex_ type specimen was sold to the [Carnegie Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Museum_of_Natural_History "Carnegie Museum of Natural History") in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, for $7,000 (equivalent to $153,224 in 2025).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-dingus2010-13) The original _Dynamosaurus_ material now resides in the collections of the [Natural History Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_History_Museum,_London "Natural History Museum, London"), London.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Breithaupt-15)_Dynamosaurus_ would later be honored by the 2018 description of another species of tyrannosaurid by Andrew McDonald and colleagues, _[Dynamoterror dynastes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamoterror\_dynastes "Dynamoterror dynastes")_, whose name was chosen in reference to the 1905 name, as it had been a "childhood favorite" of McDonald's.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-McDonald2018-16)
345|
346|From the 1910s through the end of the 1950s, Barnum's discoveries remained the only specimens of _Tyrannosaurus_, as the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") and wars kept many paleontologists out of the field.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-larson2008-8)
347|
348|### Continued study
349|
350|[![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/FMNH_SUE_Trex.jpg/250px-FMNH_SUE_Trex.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FMNH_SUE_Trex.jpg)
351|
352|Specimen "[Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)")", [Field Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History"), Chicago (with some bones reconstructed)
353|
354|Beginning in the 1960s, there was renewed interest in _Tyrannosaurus_, resulting in the recovery of 42 skeletons (5–80% complete by bone count) from western North America.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-larson2008-8) In 1967, Dr. William MacMannis located and recovered the skeleton named "MOR 008", which is 15% complete by bone count and has a reconstructed skull displayed at the [Museum of the Rockies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_the_Rockies "Museum of the Rockies"). The 1990s saw numerous discoveries, with nearly twice as many finds as in all previous years, including two of the most complete skeletons found to date: [Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)") and [Stan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_(dinosaur) "Stan (dinosaur)").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-larson2008-8)
355|
356|[Sue Hendrickson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson "Sue Hendrickson"), an [amateur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur "Amateur") paleontologist, discovered the most complete (approximately 85%) and largest _Tyrannosaurus_ skeleton in the [Hell Creek Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell_Creek_Formation "Hell Creek Formation") on August 12, 1990. The specimen Sue, named after the discoverer, was the object of a legal battle over its ownership. In 1997, the litigation was settled in favor of Maurice Williams, the original land owner. The fossil collection was purchased by the [Field Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") at auction for $7.6 million, making it the most expensive dinosaur skeleton until the sale of Stan for $31.8 million in 2020.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-17) From 1998 to 1999, Field Museum of Natural History staff spent over 25,000 hours taking the rock off the bones.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Sueprep-18) The bones were then shipped to [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") where the mount was constructed, then shipped back to Chicago for the final assembly. The mounted skeleton opened to the public on May 17, 2000, in the Field Museum of Natural History. A study of this specimen's fossilized bones showed that Sue reached full size at age 19 and died at the age of 28, the longest estimated life of any tyrannosaur known.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Ericksonetal2004TyrannosaurGigantism-19)
357|
358|[![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Scotty_Tyrannosaurus.jpg/250px-Scotty_Tyrannosaurus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scotty_Tyrannosaurus.jpg)
359|

{"content": "550|A conference abstract published in 2016 posited that theropods such as _Tyrannosaurus_ had their upper teeth covered in lips, instead of bare teeth as seen in [crocodilians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodilia "Crocodilia"). This was based on the presence of [enamel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tooth_enamel "Tooth enamel"), which according to the study needs to remain hydrated, an issue not faced by aquatic animals like crocodilians.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-:0-57) However, there has been criticism where it favors the idea for lips, with the 2017 analytical study proposing that tyrannosaurids had large, flat scales on their snouts instead of lips, as modern crocodiles do.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carr2017-55)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-naish2018-130) But crocodiles possess rather cracked keratinized skin, not flat scales; by observing the hummocky rugosity of tyrannosaurids, and comparing it to extant lizards, researchers have found that tyrannosaurids had squamose scales rather than a crocodillian-like skin.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-MontevialeCroc-58)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-131)
551|
552|In 2023, Cullen and colleagues supported the idea that theropods like tyrannosaurids had lips based on anatomical patterns, such as those of the foramina on their face and jaws, more similar to those of modern [squamates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squamate "Squamate") such as [monitor lizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monitor_lizard "Monitor lizard") or [marine iguanas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_iguana "Marine iguana") than those of modern [crocodilians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodilia "Crocodilia") like [alligators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alligator "Alligator"). Comparison of the teeth of _Daspletosaurus_ and [American alligators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_alligator "American alligator") shows that the enamel of tyrannosaurids had no significant wear and that the teeth of modern crocodilians were eroded on the labial side and were substantially worn. This suggests that it is likely that theropod teeth were kept wet by lips. On the basis of the relationship between hydration and wear resistance, the authors argued that it is unlikely that the teeth of theropods, including tyrannosaurids, would have remained unworn when exposed for a long time, because it would have been hard to maintain hydration. The authors also performed regression analyses to demonstrate the relationship between tooth height and skull length, and found that [varanids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varanid "Varanid") like the [crocodile monitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodile_monitor "Crocodile monitor") had substantially greater ratios of tooth height to skull length than those of _Tyrannosaurus_, indicating that the teeth of theropods were not too big to be covered by extraoral tissues when the mouth was closed.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-CullenEtAl23-59)
553|
554|### Sexual dimorphism
555|
556|[![Image 51](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/MUJA_04.jpg/250px-MUJA_04.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MUJA_04.jpg)
557|
558|Skeleton casts mounted in a mating position, [Jurassic Museum of Asturias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurassic_Museum_of_Asturias "Jurassic Museum of Asturias")
559|
560|As the number of known specimens increased, scientists began to analyze the variation between individuals and discovered what appeared to be two distinct body types, or _morphs_, similar to some other theropod species. As one of these morphs was more solidly built, it was termed the 'robust' morph while the other was termed '[gracile](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/gracile "wikt:gracile")'. Several [morphological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphology_(biology) "Morphology (biology)") differences associated with the two morphs were used to analyze [sexual dimorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_dimorphism "Sexual dimorphism") in _T. rex_, with the 'robust' morph usually suggested to be female. For example, the [pelvis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelvis "Pelvis") of several 'robust' specimens seemed to be wider, perhaps to allow the passage of [eggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egg_(biology) "Egg (biology)").[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carpenter1990-132) It was also thought that the 'robust' morphology correlated with a reduced [chevron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevron_(anatomy) "Chevron (anatomy)") on the first tail vertebra, also ostensibly to allow eggs to pass out of the [reproductive tract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproductive_system "Reproductive system"), as had been erroneously reported for [crocodiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodile "Crocodile").[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-larson1994-133)
561|
562|In recent years, evidence for sexual dimorphism has been weakened. A 2005 study reported that previous claims of sexual dimorphism in crocodile chevron anatomy were in error, casting doubt on the existence of similar dimorphism between _T. rex_ sexes.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-ericksonetal2005-134) A full-sized chevron was discovered on the first tail vertebra of Sue, an extremely robust individual, indicating that this feature could not be used to differentiate the two morphs anyway. As _T. rex_ specimens have been found from [Saskatchewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskatchewan "Saskatchewan") to [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico"), differences between individuals may be indicative of geographic variation rather than sexual dimorphism. The differences could also be age-related, with 'robust' individuals being older animals.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)
563|
564|Only a single _Tyrannosaurus_ specimen has been conclusively shown to belong to a specific sex. Examination of B-rex demonstrated the preservation of [soft tissue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_tissue "Soft tissue") within several bones. Some of this tissue has been identified as a medullary tissue, a specialized tissue grown only in modern birds as a source of [calcium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium "Calcium") for the production of [eggshell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eggshell "Eggshell") during [ovulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovulation "Ovulation"). As only female birds lay eggs, medullary tissue is only found naturally in females, although males are capable of producing it when injected with female reproductive [hormones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hormone "Hormone") like [estrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estrogen "Estrogen"). This strongly suggests that B-rex was female and that she died during ovulation.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-schweitzeretal2005-116) Recent research has shown that medullary tissue is never found in [crocodilians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodilian "Crocodilian"), which are thought to be the closest living relatives of dinosaurs. The shared presence of medullary tissue in birds and other theropod dinosaurs is further evidence of the close [evolutionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolution "Evolution") relationship between the two.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-schweitzeretal2007-135)
565|
566|### Posture
567|
568|[![Image 52](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/T._rex_old_posture.jpg/250px-T._rex_old_posture.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:T._rex_old_posture.jpg)
569|
570|Outdated reconstruction (by [Charles R. Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_R._Knight "Charles R. Knight")), showing upright pose
571|
572|Like many [bipedal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipedal "Bipedal") dinosaurs, _T. rex_ was historically depicted as a 'living tripod', with the body at 45 degrees or less from the vertical and the tail dragging along the ground, similar to a [kangaroo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangaroo "Kangaroo"). This concept dates from [Joseph Leidy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Leidy "Joseph Leidy")'s 1865 reconstruction of _[Hadrosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrosaurus "Hadrosaurus")_, the first to depict a dinosaur in a bipedal posture.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-leidy1865-136) In 1915, convinced that the creature stood upright, [Henry Fairfield Osborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Fairfield_Osborn "Henry Fairfield Osborn"), former president of the American Museum of Natural History, further reinforced the notion in unveiling the first complete _T. rex_ skeleton arranged this way. It stood in an upright pose for 77 years, until it was dismantled in 1992.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-amnhsite-137)
573|
574|By 1970, scientists realized this pose was incorrect and could not have been maintained by a living animal, as it would have resulted in the [dislocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dislocation_(medicine) "Dislocation (medicine)") or weakening of several [joints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint "Joint"), including the hips and the articulation between the head and the [spinal column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinal_column "Spinal column").[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-newman1970-138) The inaccurate AMNH mount inspired similar depictions in many films and paintings (such as [Rudolph Zallinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolph_F._Zallinger "Rudolph F. Zallinger")'s famous mural _[The Age of Reptiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Age\_of\_Reptiles "The Age of Reptiles")_ in [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University")'s [Peabody Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peabody_Museum_of_Natural_History "Peabody Museum of Natural History"))[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-139) until the 1990s, when films such as _[Jurassic Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurassic\_Park\_(film) "Jurassic Park (film)")_ introduced a more accurate posture to the general public.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-140) Modern representations in museums, art, and film show _T. rex_ with its body approximately parallel to the ground with the tail extended behind the body to balance the head.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-141)
575|
576|To sit down, _Tyrannosaurus_ may have settled its weight backwards and rested its weight on a pubic boot, the wide expansion at the end of the pubis in some dinosaurs. With its weight rested on the pelvis, it may have been free to move the hindlimbs. Getting back up again might have involved some stabilization from the diminutive forelimbs.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-142)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-newman1970-138) The latter known as Newman's pushup theory has been debated. Nonetheless, _Tyrannosaurus_ was probably able to get up if it fell, which only would have required placing the limbs below the center of gravity, with the tail as an effective counterbalance. Healed stress fractures in the forelimbs have been put forward both as evidence that the arms cannot have been very useful[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-143)[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Padian_(2022)-144) and as evidence that they were indeed used and acquired wounds,[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Stevens_et.al.2008-145) like the rest of the body.
577|
578|### Arms
579|
580|[![Image 53](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Tyrannosaurus_resting_pose.jpg/250px-Tyrannosaurus_resting_pose.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_resting_pose.jpg)
581|
582|The forelimbs might have been used to help _T.rex_ rise from a resting pose, as seen in this cast ([Bucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucky_(Tyrannosaurus_rex) "Bucky (Tyrannosaurus rex)") specimen)
583|
584|When _T. rex_ was first discovered, the [humerus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humerus "Humerus") was the only element of the forelimb known.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-osborn1905-12) For the initial mounted skeleton as seen by the public in 1915, Osborn substituted longer, three-fingered forelimbs like those of _[Allosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allosaurus "Allosaurus")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-osborn1917-7) A year earlier, [Lawrence Lambe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Lambe "Lawrence Lambe") described the short, two-fingered forelimbs of the closely related _Gorgosaurus_.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-lambe1914-146) This strongly suggested that _T. rex_ had similar forelimbs, but this [hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothesis "Hypothesis") was not confirmed until the first complete _T. rex_ forelimbs were identified in 1989, belonging to MOR 555 (the "Wankel rex").[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-hornerlessem1993-147)[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-148) The remains of Sue also include complete forelimbs.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)_T. rex_ arms are very small relative to overall body size, measuring only 1 meter (3.3 ft) long, and some scholars have labelled them as [vestigial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestigial_organs "Vestigial organs"). However, the bones show large areas for [muscle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscle "Muscle") attachment, indicating considerable strength. This was recognized as early as 1906 by Osborn, who speculated that the forelimbs may have been used to grasp a mate during [copulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copulation_(zoology) "Copulation (zoology)").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-osborn1906-14) Newman (1970) suggested that the forelimbs were used to assist _Ty... [truncated]
585|
586|[![Image 54](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Tyrannosaur_arm_104.JPG/250px-Tyrannosaur_arm_104.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaur_arm_104.JPG)
587|
588|Diagram illustrating arm anatomy
589|
590|Another possibility is that the forelimbs held struggling prey while it was killed by the tyrannosaur's enormous jaws. This hypothesis may be supported by [biomechanical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomechanics "Biomechanics") analysis. _T. rex_ forelimb bones exhibit extremely thick [cortical bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone#Structure "Bone"), which has been interpreted as evidence that they were developed to withstand heavy loads. The [biceps brachii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biceps_brachii "Biceps brachii") muscle of an adult _T. rex_ was capable of lifting 199 kilograms (439 lb) by itself; other muscles such as the [brachialis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brachialis "Brachialis") would work along with the biceps to make elbow flexion even more powerful. The [M. biceps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._biceps "M. biceps") muscle of _T.rex_ was 3.5 times as powerful as the [human equivalent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_equivalent "Human equivalent"). A _T. rex_ forearm had a limited range of motion, with the shoulder and elbow joints allowing only 40 and 45 degrees of motion, respectively. In contrast, the same two joints in _[Deinonychus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinonychus "Deinonychus")_ allow up to 88 and 130 degrees of motion, respectively, while a human arm can rotate 360 degrees at the shoulder and move through 165 degrees at the elbow. The heavy build of the arm bones, strength of the muscles, and limited range of motion may indicate a system evolved to hold fast despite the stresses of a struggling prey animal. In the first detailed scientific description of _Tyrannosaurus_ forelimbs, paleontologists Kenneth Carpenter and Matt Smith dismissed notions that the forelimbs were useless or that _Tyrannosaurus_ was an obligate scavenger.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carpentersmith2001-149)
591|
592|The idea that the arms served as weapons when hunting prey have also been proposed by [Steven M. Stanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_M._Stanley "Steven M. Stanley"), who suggested that the arms were used for slashing prey, especially by using the claws to rapidly inflict long, deep gashes to its prey.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-150) This was dismissed by Padian, who argued that Stanley based his conclusion on incorrectly estimated forelimb size and range of motion.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Padian_(2022)-144)
593|
594|### Thermoregulation
595|
596|Main article: [Physiology of dinosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology_of_dinosaurs "Physiology of dinosaurs")
597|
598|[![Image 55](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Tyrannosaurus_rex_mmartyniuk.png/250px-Tyrannosaurus_rex_mmartyniuk.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_rex_mmartyniuk.png)
599|
600|Restoration showing partial feathering
601|
602|_Tyrannosaurus_, like most dinosaurs, was long thought to have an [ectothermic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ectotherm "Ectotherm") ("cold-blooded") reptilian [metabolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolism "Metabolism"). The idea of dinosaur ectothermy was challenged by scientists like [Robert T. Bakker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_T._Bakker "Robert T. Bakker") and [John Ostrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ostrom "John Ostrom") in the early years of the "[dinosaur renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur_renaissance "Dinosaur renaissance")", beginning in the late 1960s.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-bakker1968-151)[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-bakker1972-152)_T. rex_ itself was claimed to have been [endothermic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warm-blooded "Warm-blooded") ("warm-blooded"), implying a very active lifestyle.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-bakker1986-39) Since then, several paleontologists have sought to determine the ability of _Tyrannosaurus_ to [regulate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermoregulation "Thermoregulation") its body temperature. Histological evidence of high growth rates in young _T. rex_, comparable to those of mammals and birds, may support the hypothesis of a high metabolism. Growth curves indicate that, as in mammals and birds, _T. rex_ growth was limited mostly to immature animals, rather than the [indeterminate growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indeterminate_growth "Indeterminate growth") seen in most other [vertebrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebrate "Vertebrate").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-hornerpadian2004-115)
603|
604|[Oxygen isotope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotopes_of_oxygen "Isotopes of oxygen") ratios in fossilized bone are sometimes used to determine the temperature at which the bone was deposited, as the ratio between certain isotopes correlates with temperature. In one specimen, the isotope ratios in bones from different parts of the body indicated a temperature difference of no more than 4 to 5°C (7 to 9°F) between the vertebrae of the torso and the [tibia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibia "Tibia") of the lower leg. This small temperature range between the body core and the extremities was claimed by paleontologist Reese Barrick and [geochemist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geochemistry "Geochemistry") William Showers to indicate that _T. rex_ maintained a constant internal body temperature ([homeothermy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeotherm "Homeotherm")) and that it enjoyed a metabolism somewhere between ectothermic reptiles and endothermic mammals.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-barrettshowers1994-153) Other scientists have pointed out that the ratio of oxygen isotopes in the fossils today does not necessarily represent the same ratio in the distant past, and may have been altered during or after fossilization ([diagenesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagenesis "Diagenesis")).[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-truemanetal2003-154) Barrick and Showers have defended their conclusions in subsequent papers, finding similar results in another theropod dinosaur from a different continent and tens of millions of years earlier in time (_[Giganotosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giganotosaurus "Giganotosaurus")_).[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-barrickshowers1999-155)[Ornithischian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornithischia "Ornithischia") dinosaurs also showed evidence of homeothermy, while [varanid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varanidae "Varanidae") lizards from the... [truncated]

606|Even if _T. rex_ does exhibit evidence of homeothermy, it does not necessarily mean that it was endothermic. Such thermoregulation may also be explained by [gigantothermy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigantothermy "Gigantothermy"), as in some living [sea turtles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_turtle "Sea turtle").[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-paladinoetal1997-158)[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-chinsamyhillenius2004-159)[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-160) Similar to contemporary crocodilians, openings (dorsotemporal fenestrae) in the skull roofs of _Tyrannosaurus_ may have aided thermoregulation.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-holliday2019-161)

614|In the March 2005 issue of _[Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science\_(journal) "Science (journal)")_, [Mary Higby Schweitzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Higby_Schweitzer "Mary Higby Schweitzer") of [North Carolina State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_State_University "North Carolina State University") and colleagues announced the recovery of soft tissue from the marrow cavity of a fossilized leg bone from a _T. rex_. The bone had been intentionally, though reluctantly, broken for shipping and then not preserved in the normal manner, specifically because Schweitzer was hoping to test it for soft tissue.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-smithsonian-fields-162) Designated as the Museum of the Rockies specimen 1125, or MOR 1125, the dinosaur was previously excavated from the [Hell Creek Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell_Creek_Formation "Hell Creek Formation"). Flexible, bifurcating [blood vessels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_vessel "Blood vessel") and fibrous but elastic [bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone "Bone") matrix tissue were recognized. In addition, microstructures resembling [blood cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_cell "Blood cell") were found inside the matrix and vessels. The structures bear resemblance to [ostrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrich "Ostrich") blood cells and vessels. Whether an unknown process, distinct from normal fossilization, preserved the material, or the material is original, the researchers do not know, and they are careful not to make any claims about preservation.[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-MHSetalb-163) If it is found to be original material, any surviving proteins may be used as a means of indirectly guessing some of the DNA content of the dinosaurs involved, because each protein is typically created by a specific gene. The absence of previous finds may be the result of people assuming pre... [truncated]
615|
616|In studies reported in _Science_ in April 2007, Asara and colleagues concluded that seven traces of [collagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collagen "Collagen") proteins detected in purified _T. rex_ bone most closely match those reported in [chickens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicken "Chicken"), followed by frogs and newts. The discovery of proteins from a creature tens of millions of years old, along with similar traces the team found in a mastodon bone at least 160,000 years old, upends the conventional view of fossils and may shift paleontologists' focus from bone hunting to biochemistry.[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] Until these finds, most scientists presumed that fossilization replaced all living tissue with inert minerals. Paleontologist Hans Larsson of McGill University in Montreal, who was not part of the studies, called the finds "a milestone", and suggested that dinosaurs could "enter the field of molecular biology and really slingshot paleontology into the modern world".[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-166)
617|
618|The presumed soft tissue was called into question by Thomas Kaye of the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") and his co-authors in 2008. They contend that what was really inside the tyrannosaur bone was slimy [biofilm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biofilm "Biofilm") created by bacteria that coated the voids once occupied by blood vessels and cells.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-167) The researchers found that what previously had been identified as remnants of blood cells, because of the presence of iron, were actually [framboids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Framboid "Framboid"), microscopic mineral spheres bearing iron. They found similar spheres in a variety of other fossils from various periods, including an [ammonite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonite "Ammonite"). In the ammonite, they found the spheres in a place where the iron they contain could not have had any relationship to the presence of blood.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-168) Schweitzer has strongly criticized Kaye's claims and argues that there is no reported evidence that biofilms can produce branching, hollow tubes like those noted in her study.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-169) San Antonio, Schweitzer and colleagues published an analysis in 2011 of what parts of the collagen had been recovered, finding that it was the inner parts of the collagen coil that had been preserved, as would have been expected from a long period of protein degradation.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-170) Other research challenges the identification of soft tissue as biofilm and confirms finding "branching, vessel-like structures" from within fossilized bone.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-171)

640|Scientists have produced a wide range of possible maximum running speeds for _Tyrannosaurus_: mostly around 9 meters per second (32 km/h; 20 mph), but as low as 4.5–6.8 meters per second (16–24 km/h; 10–15 mph) and as high as 20 meters per second (72 km/h; 45 mph). According to John Hutchinson and colleagues, _Tyrannosaurus_ was unlikely to run fast .[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-HutchinsonGarcia2002TrexSlow-172)

642|A 2002 report used a mathematical model (validated by applying it to three living animals: [alligators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alligator "Alligator"), [chickens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicken "Chicken"), and [humans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human "Human"); and eight more species, including emus and ostriches[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Hutchinson2004-173)) to gauge the leg muscle mass needed for fast running (over 40 km/h or 25 mph).[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-HutchinsonGarcia2002TrexSlow-172) Scientists who think that _Tyrannosaurus_ was able to run point out that hollow bones and other features that would have lightened its body may have kept adult weight to a mere 4.5 metric tons (5.0 short tons) or so, or that other animals like [ostriches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostrich "Ostrich") and [horses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse "Horse") with long, flexible legs are able to achieve high speeds through slower but longer strides.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Hutchinson2004-173) Proposed top speeds exceeded 40 kilometers per hour (25 mph) for _Tyrannosaurus_, but were deemed infeasible because they would require exceptional leg muscles of approximately 40–86%of total body mass. Even moderately fast speeds would have required large leg muscles. If the muscle mass was less, only 18 kilometers per hour (11 mph) for walking or jogging would have been possible.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-HutchinsonGarcia2002TrexSlow-172) Holtz noted that tyrannosaurids and some closely related groups had significantly longer [distal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distal "Distal") hindlimb components (shin plus foot plus toes) relative to the femur length than most other theropods, and that tyrannosaurids and their close relatives had a tightly interlocked [metatarsus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metatarsus "Metatarsus") (foot... 648|Additionally, a 2020 study indicates that _Tyrannosaurus_ and other tyrannosaurids were exceptionally efficient walkers. Studies by Dececchi et al., compared the leg proportions, body mass, and the gaits of more than 70 species of theropod dinosaurs including _Tyrannosaurus_ and its relatives. The research team then applied a variety of methods to estimate each dinosaur's top speed when running as well as how much energy each dinosaur expended while moving at more relaxed speeds such as when walking. Among smaller to medium-sized species such as dromaeosaurids, longer legs appear to be an adaptation for faster running, in line with previous results by other researchers. But for theropods weighing over 1,000 kg (2,200 lb), top running speed is limited by body size, so longer legs instead were found to have correlated with low-energy walking. The results further indicate that smaller theropods evolved long legs as a means to both aid in hunting and escape from larger predators while larger theropods that evolved long legs did so to reduce the energy costs and increase foraging efficiency, as they were freed from the demands of predation pressure due to their role as apex predators. Compared to more basal groups of theropods in the study, tyrannosaurs like _Tyrannosaurus_ itself showed a marked increase in foraging efficiency due to reduced energy expenditures during hunting or scavenging. This in turn likely resulted in tyrannosaurs having a reduced need for hunting forays and requiring less food to sustain themselves as a result. Additionally, the research, in conjunction with studies that show tyrannosaurs were more agile than other large-bodied theropods, indicates they were quite well-adapted to a long-distance stalking approach followed by a quick burst of speed to go for the kill. Analogies can be noted between tyrannosaurids and modern wolves as a result, supported by evidence that at least some tyrannosaurids were hunting in group settings.[[175]](https://en.w... [truncated]

650|A study published in 2021 by Pasha van Bijlert et al., calculated the [preferred walking speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preferred_walking_speed "Preferred walking speed") of _Tyrannosaurus_, reporting a speed of 1.28 meters per second (4.6 km/h; 2.9 mph). While walking, animals reduce their [energy expenditure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cost_of_transport "Cost of transport") by choosing certain step rhythms at which their body parts [resonate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resonate "Resonate"). The same would have been true for [dinosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaurs "Dinosaurs"), but previous studies did not fully account for the impact the tail had on their walking speeds. According to the authors, when a dinosaur walked, its tail would slightly sway up and down with each step as a result of the [interspinous ligaments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interspinous_ligaments "Interspinous ligaments") suspending the tail. Like rubber bands, these ligaments stored energy when they are stretched due to the swaying of the tail. Using a 3-D model of _Tyrannosaurus_ specimen [Trix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trix_(dinosaur) "Trix (dinosaur)"), muscles and ligaments were reconstructed to simulate the tail movements. This results in a rhythmic, energy-efficient walking speed for _Tyrannosaurus_ similar to that seen in living animals such as humans, ostriches and giraffes.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-vanBijlert2021-178)

652|A 2017 study estimated the top running speed of _Tyrannosaurus_ as 17 mph (27 km/h), speculating that _Tyrannosaurus_ exhausted its energy reserves long before reaching top speed, resulting in a parabola-like relationship between size and speed.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-179)[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-180) Another 2017 study hypothesized that an adult _Tyrannosaurus_ was incapable of running due to high skeletal loads. Using a calculated weight estimate of 7 tons, the model showed that speeds above 11 mph (18 km/h) would have probably shattered the leg bones of _Tyrannosaurus_. The finding may mean that running was also not possible for other giant theropod dinosaurs like _[Giganotosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giganotosaurus "Giganotosaurus")_, _[Mapusaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mapusaurus "Mapusaurus")_ and _[Acrocanthosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acrocanthosaurus "Acrocanthosaurus")_.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-181) However, studies by Eric Snively and colleagues _,_ published in 2019 indicate that _Tyrannosaurus_ and other tyrannosaurids were more maneuverable than allosauroids and other theropods of comparable size due to low rotational inertia compared to their body mass combined with large leg muscles. As a result, it is hypothesized that _Tyrannosaurus_ was capable of making relatively quick turns and could likely pivot its body more quickly when close to its prey, or that while turning, the theropod could "pirouette" on a single planted foot while the alternating leg was held out in a suspended swing during a pursuit. 660|Two isolated fossilized [footprints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footprint "Footprint") have been tentatively assigned to _T. rex_. The first was discovered at [Philmont Scout Ranch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philmont_Scout_Ranch "Philmont Scout Ranch"), New Mexico, in 1983 by American geologist Charles Pillmore. Originally thought to belong to a [hadrosaurid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrosaurid "Hadrosaurid"), examination of the footprint revealed a large 'heel' unknown in [ornithopod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornithopod "Ornithopod") dinosaur tracks, and traces of what may have been a [hallux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallux "Hallux"), the dewclaw-like fourth digit of the tyrannosaur foot. The footprint was published as the [ichnogenus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ichnogenus "Ichnogenus")_[Tyrannosauripus pillmorei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosauripus\_pillmorei "Tyrannosauripus pillmorei")_ in 1994, by [Martin Lockley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Lockley "Martin Lockley") and Adrian Hunt. Lockley and Hunt suggested that it was very likely the track was made by a _T. rex_, which would make it the first known footprint from this species. The track was made in what was once a vegetated wetland mudflat. It measures 83 centimeters (33 in) long by 71 centimeters (28 in) wide.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-lockley&hunt1994-183)
661|
662|A second footprint that may have been made by a _Tyrannosaurus_ was first reported in 2007 by British paleontologist Phil Manning, from the [Hell Creek Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell_Creek_Formation "Hell Creek Formation") of Montana. This second track measures 72 centimeters (28 in) long, shorter than the track described by Lockley and Hunt. Whether or not the track was made by _Tyrannosaurus_ is unclear, though _Tyrannosaurus_ is the only large theropod known to have existed in the Hell Creek Formation.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-rextrack2007-184)[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-manningetal2008-185)
663|
664|A set of footprints in Glenrock, Wyoming dating to the [Maastrichtian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastrichtian "Maastrichtian") stage of the Late Cretaceous and hailing from the [Lance Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lance_Formation "Lance Formation") were described by Scott Persons, Phil Currie and colleagues in 2016, and are believed to belong to either a juvenile _T. rex_ or _Nanotyrannus lancensis_. From measurements and based on the positions of the footprints, the animal was believed to be traveling at a walking speed of around 2.8 to 5 miles per hour and was estimated to have a hip height of 1.56 to 2.06 m (5.1 to 6.8 ft).[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-186)[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-187)[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-188) A follow-up paper appeared in 2017, increasing the speed estimations by 50–80%.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-189)
665|
666|Rare fossil footprints and trackways found in New Mexico and Wyoming that are assigned to the ichnogenus _[Tyrannosauripus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosauripus "Tyrannosauripus")_ have been attributed to being made by _Tyrannosaurus_, based on the stratigraphic age of the rocks they are preserved in. The first specimen, found in 1994 was described by Lockley and Hunt and consists of a single, large footprint. Another pair of ichnofossils, described in 2021, show a large tyrannosaurid rising from a prone position by rising up using its elbows in conjunction with the pads on their feet to stand. These two unique sets of fossils were found in Ludlow, Colorado and Cimarron, New Mexico.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-190) Another ichnofossil described in 2018, perhaps belonging to a juvenile _Tyrannosaurus_ or _Nanotyrannus_ was uncovered in the Lance Formation of Wyoming. The trackway itself offers a rare glimpse into the walking speed of tyrannosaurids, and the trackmaker is estimated to have been moving at a speed of 4.5–8.0 kilometers per hour (2.8–5.0 mph), significantly faster than previously assumed for estimations of walking speed in tyrannosaurids.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-191)

674|A study conducted by [Lawrence Witmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Witmer "Lawrence Witmer") and Ryan Ridgely of Ohio University found that _Tyrannosaurus_ shared the heightened sensory abilities of other [coelurosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coelurosaur "Coelurosaur"), highlighting relatively rapid and coordinated eye and head movements; an enhanced ability to sense low frequency sounds, which would allow tyrannosaurs to track prey movements from long distances; and an enhanced sense of smell.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-witmer2009-192) A study published by Kent Stevens concluded that _Tyrannosaurus_ had keen vision. By applying modified [perimetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perimetry "Perimetry") to facial reconstructions of several dinosaurs including _Tyrannosaurus_, the study found that _Tyrannosaurus_ had a binocular range of 55 degrees, surpassing that of modern hawks. Stevens estimated that _Tyrannosaurus_ had 13 times the visual acuity of a human and surpassed the visual acuity of an eagle, which is 3.6 times that of a person. Stevens estimated a limiting far point (that is, the distance at which an object can be seen as separate from the horizon) as far as 6 km (3.7 mi) away, which is greater than the 1.6 km (1 mi) that a human can see.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Stevens2006Binocular-46)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-jaffe-47)[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-stevenswebpage-193)

676|Thomas Holtz Jr. would note that high depth perception of _Tyrannosaurus_ may have been due to the prey it had to hunt, noting that it had to hunt ceratopsians such as _[Triceratops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triceratops "Triceratops")_, ankylosaurs such as _[Ankylosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankylosaurus "Ankylosaurus")_, and hadrosaurs. He would suggest that this made precision more crucial for _Tyrannosaurus_ enabling it to, "get in, get that blow in and take it down." In contrast, _[Acrocanthosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acrocanthosaurus "Acrocanthosaurus")_ had limited depth perception because they hunted large sauropods, which were relatively rare during the time of _Tyrannosaurus_.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-HoltzLecture2013-124)

678|Though no _Tyrannosaurus_[scleral ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scleral_ring "Scleral ring") has been found, [Kenneth Carpenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carpenter "Kenneth Carpenter") estimated its size based on that of _Gorgosaurus_. The inferred scleral ring for the Stan specimen is ~7 cm (2.8 in) in diameter with an internal aperture diameter of ~3.5 cm (1.4 in). Based on eye proportions in living reptiles, this implies a pupil diameter of about 2.5 cm (0.98 in), an iris diameter about that of the scleral ring, and an eyeball diameter of 11–12 cm (4.3–4.7 in). Carpenter also estimated an eyeball depth of ~7.7–9.6 cm (3.0–3.8 in). Based on these calculations, the [f-number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-number "F-number") for Stan's eye is 3–3.8; since [diurnal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diurnality "Diurnality") animals have f-numbers of 2.1 or higher, this would indicate that _Tyrannosaurus_ had poor low-light vision and hunted during the day.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Trexpaleobiologychapter14-194)
679|
680|_Tyrannosaurus_ had very large [olfactory bulbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olfactory_bulb "Olfactory bulb") and [olfactory nerves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olfactory_nerve "Olfactory nerve") relative to their brain size, the organs responsible for a heightened sense of smell. This suggests that the sense of smell was highly developed, and implies that tyrannosaurs could detect carcasses by scent alone across great distances. The sense of smell in tyrannosaurs may have been comparable to modern [vultures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulture "Vulture"), which use scent to track carcasses for scavenging. Research on the olfactory bulbs has shown that _T. rex_ had the most highly developed sense of smell of 21 sampled non-avian dinosaur species.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Calgary_Herald-195)

686|Somewhat unusually among theropods, _T.rex_ had a very long [cochlea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cochlea "Cochlea"). The length of the cochlea is often related to hearing acuity, or at least the importance of hearing in behavior, implying that hearing was a particularly important sense to tyrannosaurs. Specifically, data suggests that _T. rex_ heard best in the low-frequency range, and that low-frequency sounds were an important part of tyrannosaur behavior.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-witmer2009-192) A 2017 study by Thomas Carr and colleagues found that the snout of tyrannosaurids was highly sensitive, based on a high number of small openings in the facial bones of the related _Daspletosaurus_ that contained [sensory neurons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensory_neuron "Sensory neuron"). The study speculated that tyrannosaurs might have used their sensitive snouts to measure the temperature of their nests and to gently pick up eggs and hatchlings, as seen in modern crocodilians.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carr2017-55) Another study published in 2021 further suggests that _Tyrannosaurus_ had an acute sense of touch, based on neurovascular canals in the front of its jaws, which it could utilize to better detect and consume prey. The study, published by Kawabe and Hittori et al., suggests that _Tyrannosaurus_ could also accurately sense slight differences in material and movement, allowing it to utilize different feeding strategies on different parts of its prey's carcasses depending on the situation. The sensitive neurovascular canals of _Tyrannosaurus_ also likely were adapted to performing fine movements and behaviors such as nest building, parental care, and other social behavior such as intraspecific communication. The results of this study also align with results made in studying the related tyrannosaurid _[Daspletosaurus horneri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daspletosaurus\_horneri "Daspleto... [truncated]
687|
688|A study by Grant R. Hurlburt, Ryan C. Ridgely and Lawrence Witmer obtained estimates for [Encephalization Quotients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encephalization_Quotient "Encephalization Quotient") (EQs), based on reptiles and birds, as well as estimates for the ratio of cerebrum to brain mass. The study concluded that _Tyrannosaurus_ had the relatively largest brain of all adult non-avian dinosaurs with the exception of certain small maniraptoriforms (_[Bambiraptor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bambiraptor "Bambiraptor")_, _[Troodon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troodon "Troodon")_ and _[Ornithomimus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornithomimus "Ornithomimus")_). The study found that _Tyrannosaurus'_ s relative brain size was still within the range of modern reptiles, being at most 2 [standard deviations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_deviations "Standard deviations") above the mean of non-avian reptile EQs. The estimates for the ratio of cerebrum mass to brain mass would range from 47.5 to 49.53 percent. According to the study, this is more than the lowest estimates for extant birds (44.6 percent), but still close to the typical ratios of the smallest sexually mature alligators which range from 45.9 to 47.9 percent.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Trexpaleobiologychapter6-199) Other studies, such as those by Steve Brusatte, indicate the encephalization quotient of _Tyrannosaurus_ was similar in range (2.0–2.4) to a [chimpanzee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimpanzee "Chimpanzee") (2.2–2.5), though this may be debatable as reptilian and mammalian encephalization quotients are not equivalent.[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-200)

696|[Philip J. Currie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_J._Currie "Philip J. Currie") suggested that Tyrannosaurus may have been [pack hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pack_hunter "Pack hunter"), comparing _T. rex_ to related species _[Tarbosaurus bataar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarbosaurus\_bataar "Tarbosaurus bataar")_ and _[Albertosaurus sarcophagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albertosaurus\_sarcophagus "Albertosaurus sarcophagus")_, citing fossil evidence that may indicate [gregarious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociality "Sociality") (describing animals that travel in herds or packs) behavior.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-discoverdinogangs-201) A find in [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota") where three _T. rex_ skeletons were in close proximity may suggest the formation of a pack.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-tgraphpack-202)[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-djournal-203) Cooperative pack hunting may have been an effective strategy for subduing prey with advanced [anti-predator adaptations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-predator_adaptation "Anti-predator adaptation") which pose potential lethality such as _[Triceratops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triceratops "Triceratops")_ and _[Ankylosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankylosaurus "Ankylosaurus")_.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-discoverdinogangs-201)
697|
698|Currie's pack-hunting _T. rex_ hypothesis has been criticized for not having been [peer-reviewed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peer-review "Peer-review"), but rather was discussed in a television interview and book called _Dino Gangs_.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-switek2011dinogangs-204) The Currie theory for pack hunting by _T. rex_ is based mainly by analogy to a different species, _Tarbosaurus bataar_. Evidence of gregariousness in _T. bataar_ itself has not been peer-reviewed, and to Currie's own admission, can only be interpreted with reference to evidence in other closely related species. According to Currie gregariousness in _Albertosaurus sarcophagus_ is supported by the discovery of 26 individuals with varied ages in the Dry Island bonebed. He ruled out the possibility of a predator trap due to the similar preservation state of individuals and the near absence of herbivores.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-switek2011dinogangs-204)[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-currie1998-205)
699|
700|Additional support of tyrannosaurid gregariousness can be found in fossilized [trackways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trackway "Trackway") from the Upper Cretaceous [Wapiti Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wapiti_Formation "Wapiti Formation") of northeastern [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia"), Canada, left by three tyrannosaurids traveling in the same direction.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-TG-20140724-206)[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-207) According to scientists assessing the Dino Gangs program, the evidence for pack hunting in _Tarbosaurus_ and _Albertosaurus_ is weak and based on group skeletal remains for which alternate explanations may apply (such as drought or a flood forcing dinosaurs to die together in one place).[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-switek2011dinogangs-204) Others researchers have speculated that instead of large theropod social groups, some of these finds represent behavior more akin to [Komodo dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komodo_dragon "Komodo dragon")-like mobbing of carcasses, even going as far as to say true pack-hunting behavior may not exist in any non-avian dinosaurs due to its rarity in modern predators.[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-roachbrinkman2007-208) Pathologies of _Tyrannosaurus_ specimens have been suggested as evidence of conspecific attack, including "Wyrex" with a hole penetrating its jugual and severe trauma on its tail that shows signs of [bone remodeling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_remodeling "Bone remodeling") (not regrowth).[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Trexpaleobiologychapter10-209)[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-210)

714|A discredited fringe hypothesis that was never seriously considered was that _Tyrannosaurus_ was an obligate [scavenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scavenger "Scavenger"). The argument originated in a 1917 study by Lambe which argued that large theropods were pure scavengers because _Gorgosaurus_ teeth showed hardly any wear.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Lambe1917Gorgosaurus-220) This argument disregarded the fact that theropods replaced their teeth quite rapidly. Ever since the first discovery of _Tyrannosaurus_ most scientists have agreed that it was an active predator, though like modern large predators it would readily scavenge or steal another predator's kill if it had the opportunity.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-FarlowHoltz2002FossilRecordPredation-221)[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-222)

716|Paleontologist [Jack Horner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Horner_(paleontologist) "Jack Horner (paleontologist)") has been a major proponent of the view that _Tyrannosaurus_ was not a predator at all but instead was an obligate scavenger.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-hornerlessem1993-147)[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Horner1994SteakKnives-223)[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-BBC2003TrexOnTrial-224) He has put forward arguments in the popular literature to support the pure scavenger hypothesis:

722|*   Tyrannosaur arms are short when compared to other known predators. Horner argues that the arms were too short to make the necessary gripping force to hold on to prey.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-BBC2003TrexOnTrial-224) Other paleontologists such as [Thomas Holtz Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_R._Holtz_Jr. "Thomas R. Holtz Jr.") pointed out that there are plenty of modern-day predators that do not use their forelimbs to hunt such as [wolves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf "Wolf"), [hyenas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyena "Hyena"), and [secretary birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretarybird "Secretarybird") as well as other extinct animals thought to be predators that would not have used their forelimbs such as [phorusrhacids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phorusrhacidae "Phorusrhacidae").[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-FarlowHoltz2002FossilRecordPredation2-225)[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Tyrantkingbook-226)
723|*   Tyrannosaurs had large [olfactory bulbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olfactory_bulb "Olfactory bulb") and [olfactory nerves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olfactory_nerve "Olfactory nerve") (relative to their brain size). These suggest a highly developed sense of smell which could sniff out carcasses over great distances, as modern [vultures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulture "Vulture") do. Research on the olfactory bulbs of dinosaurs has shown that _Tyrannosaurus_ had the most highly developed sense of smell of 21 sampled dinosaurs.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Calgary_Herald-195) However, good olfactory capabilities are also common in predatory animals, so this fails to provide evidence against predatory behavior.[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-227)
724|*   Tyrannosaur teeth could crush bone, and therefore could extract as much food ([bone marrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_marrow "Bone marrow")) as possible from carcass remnants, usually the least nutritious parts. Karen Chin and colleagues have found bone fragments in [coprolites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coprolite "Coprolite") (fossilized feces) that they attribute to tyrannosaurs, but point out that a tyrannosaur's teeth were not well adapted to systematically chewing bone like [hyenas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyena "Hyena") do to extract marrow.[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-ChinEtal1998KingSizeCoprolite-228)
725|*   Since at least some of _Tyrannosaurus_'s potential prey could move quickly, evidence that it walked instead of ran could indicate that it was a scavenger.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Horner1994SteakKnives-223) However, most analyses indicate _Tyrannosaurus_, while slower than large modern terrestrial predators due to being far larger, was still faster than large [hadrosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrosaurs "Hadrosaurs") and [ceratopsians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceratopsians "Ceratopsians").[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-HutchinsonGarcia2002TrexSlow-172)[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-manningetal2008-185)[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-229)

727|Most evidence suggests hunting behavior in _Tyrannosaurus_. The eye sockets of tyrannosaurs are positioned so that the eyes would point forward, giving them [binocular vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binocular_vision "Binocular vision") slightly better than that of modern [hawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawk "Hawk"). It is not obvious why [natural selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_selection "Natural selection") would have favored this long-term trend if tyrannosaurs had been pure scavengers, which would not have needed the advanced [depth perception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth_perception "Depth perception") that [stereoscopic vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereoscopic_vision "Stereoscopic vision") provides.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Stevens2006Binocular-46)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-jaffe-47) In modern animals, binocular vision is found mainly in predators (though not all predators have well-developed binocular vision).

735|In 1992, [William Abler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Abler "William Abler") suggested that _Tyrannosaurus_ may have had infectious [saliva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saliva "Saliva") used to kill its prey. Abler observed that the [serrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_dinosaur_anatomy#serrations "Glossary of dinosaur anatomy") (tiny protuberances) on the cutting edges of the teeth are closely spaced, enclosing little chambers, which he argued trapped pieces of carcass with bacteria, giving _Tyrannosaurus_ a deadly, infectious bite, as the [Komodo dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komodo_dragon "Komodo dragon") was mistakenly thought to have.[[238]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-abler1992-239) Jack Horner and Don Lessem, in a 1993 popular book, questioned Abler's hypothesis, arguing that _Tyrannosaurus_'s tooth serrations as more like cubes in shape than the serrations on a Komodo monitor's teeth, which are rounded.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-hornerlessem1993-147):214–215 The basis for an infectious bite in _Tyrannosaurus_ or any other theropod was further undermined when it was found Komodo dragons do not actually have an infectious bite nor hunt by biting prey and tracking it as it weakens.[[239]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-goldstein2013-240)

737|_Tyrannosaurus_ probably primarily processed carcasses with lateral shakes of the head, like crocodilians. The head was not as maneuverable as the skulls of [allosauroids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allosauroidea "Allosauroidea"), due to flat joints of the neck vertebrae.[[240]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-ESetal2013-241)[[241]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-242) Studies on hadrosaur vertebrae from the Hell Creek Formation that were punctured by the teeth of what appears to be a late-stage juvenile _Tyrannosaurus_ indicate that despite lacking the bone-crushing adaptations of the adults, young individuals were still capable of using the same bone-puncturing feeding technique as their adult counterparts.[[242]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Peterson-243)

739|Evidence also strongly suggests that tyrannosaurs were at least occasionally cannibalistic. _Tyrannosaurus_ itself has strong evidence pointing towards it having been cannibalistic in at least a scavenging capacity based on tooth marks on the foot bones, humerus, and metatarsals of one specimen.[[243]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-HornerCurrie_et.al._2010_Trex_cannibalism-244)
