741|### Parenting
742|
743|While there is no direct evidence of _Tyrannosaurus_ raising their young (the rarity of juvenile and nest Tyrannosaur fossils has left researchers guessing), it has been suggested that like its closest living relatives, birds and crocodiles (modern archosaurs), _Tyrannosaurus_ may have protected and fed its young. Crocodilians and birds are often suggested by some paleontologists to be modern analogues for dinosaur parenting.[[244]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-245) Direct evidence of parental behavior exists in other dinosaurs such as _[Maiasaura peeblesorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiasaura "Maiasaura")_, the first dinosaur to have been discovered to raise its young, as well as more closely related [Oviraptorids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oviraptoridae "Oviraptoridae"), the latter suggesting parental behavior in theropods.[[245]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-246)[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-247)[[247]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-248)[[248]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-249)[[249]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-250) Some very young specimens assigned to _Tyrannosaurus rex_ suggest that, although the species may have provided parental care, it was likely limited and did not reach the level of care seen in modern birds.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Longrich2026-123)

{"content": "380|Size (in blue) compared to select giant theropods and a human
381|
382|_T. rex_ was one of the largest land carnivores of all time. One of its largest and the most complete specimens, nicknamed [Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)") (FMNH PR2081), is located at the [Field Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") in Chicago. Sue measured 12.3–12.8 m (40–42 ft) long,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-SueFMNH-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Hutchinsonet.al.2011-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Holtz2008-31) was 3.66–3.96 m (12.0–13.0 ft) tall at the hips,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-SueFMNH-29)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Sue-32)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-FMNH-33) and according to the most recent studies, using a variety of techniques, maximum body masses have been estimated approximately 8.4–9.22 t (8.27–9.07 long tons; 9.26–10.16 short tons).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Persons-34)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-HartmanMassEstimate-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-nicolas2014-36) A specimen nicknamed [Scotty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotty_(dinosaur) "Scotty (dinosaur)") (RSM P2523.8), located at the [Royal Saskatchewan Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Saskatchewan_Museum "Royal Saskatchewan Museum"), is reported to measure 13 m (43 ft) in length. Using a mass estimation technique that extrapolates from the [circumference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumference "Circumference") of the femur, Scotty was estimated as the largest known specimen at 8.87 t (8.73 long tons; 9.78 short tons) in body mass.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Persons-34)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Ly... [truncated]
383|
384|Not every adult _Tyrannosaurus_ specimen recovered is as big. Historically average adult mass estimates have varied widely over the years, from as low as 4.5 t (4.4 long tons; 5.0 short tons),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-andersonetal1985-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-bakker1986-39) to more than 7.2 t (7.1 long tons; 7.9 short tons),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-henderson1999-40) with most modern estimates ranging between 5.4 and 8.0 t (5.3 and 7.9 long tons; 6.0 and 8.8 short tons).[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Hutchinsonet.al.2011-30)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-ericksonetal2004-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-farlowetal1995-42)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-seebacher2001-43)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-christiansenfarina2004-44)

394|The largest known _T. rex_ skulls measure up to 1.52 m (5 ft 0 in) in length.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-MOR008-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-SueFMNH-29) Large [fenestrae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenestra_(anatomy) "Fenestra (anatomy)") (openings) in the skull reduced weight, as in all carnivorous theropods. In other respects _Tyrannosaurus_'s skull was significantly different from those of large non-[tyrannosaurid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurid "Tyrannosaurid") theropods. It was extremely wide at the rear but had a narrow snout, allowing unusually good [binocular vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binocular_vision "Binocular vision").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Stevens2006Binocular-46)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-jaffe-47) The skull bones were massive and the [nasals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_bone "Nasal bone") and some other bones were fused, preventing movement between them; but many were [pneumatized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumatized_bones "Pneumatized bones") (contained a "honeycomb" of tiny air spaces) and thus lighter. These and other skull-strengthening features are part of the [tyrannosaurid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurid "Tyrannosaurid") trend towards an increasingly powerful bite, which easily surpassed that of all non-tyrannosaurids.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-SnivelyHendersonPhillips2006FusedVaultedNasals-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-MM03-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-GEetal96-50) The tip of the upper jaw was U-shaped (most non-tyrannosauroid carnivores had V-shaped upper jaws), which increased the amount of tissue and bone a tyrannosaur could rip out with one bite, although it also increased the stresses on the front teeth.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyranno... [truncated]

396|The teeth of _T. rex_ displayed marked [heterodonty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterodont "Heterodont") (differences in shape).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Smith2005HeterodontyTRex-52) The [premaxillary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premaxilla "Premaxilla") teeth, four per side at the front of the upper jaw, were closely packed, _D_-shaped in cross-section, had reinforcing ridges on the rear surface, were [incisiform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incisor "Incisor") (their tips were chisel-like blades) and curved backwards. The _D_-shaped cross-section, reinforcing ridges and backwards curve reduced the risk that the teeth would snap when _Tyrannosaurus_ bit and pulled. The remaining teeth were robust, like "lethal bananas" rather than daggers, more widely spaced and also had reinforcing ridges.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-New_Scientist1998DinosaurDetectives-53) Those in the upper jaw, twelve per side in mature individuals,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10) were larger than their counterparts of the lower jaw, except at the rear. The largest found so far is estimated to have been 30.5 cm (12.0 in) long including the root when the animal was alive, making it the largest tooth of any carnivorous dinosaur yet found.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-SueFMNH2-54) The lower jaw was robust. Its front [dentary bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dentary_bone "Dentary bone") bore thirteen teeth. Behind the tooth row, the lower jaw became notably taller.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10) The upper and lower jaws of _Tyrannosaurus_, like those of many dinosaurs, possessed numerous [foramina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foramen "Foramen"), or small holes in the bone. Various functions have been proposed for these foramina, such as... [truncated]

408|The [vertebral column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebral_column "Vertebral column") of _Tyrannosaurus_ consisted of ten neck vertebrae, thirteen back vertebrae and five sacral vertebrae. The number of tail vertebrae is unknown and could well have varied between individuals but probably numbered at least forty. Sue was mounted with forty-seven of such caudal vertebrae.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10) The neck of _T. rex_ formed a natural S-shaped curve like that of other theropods. Compared to these, it was exceptionally short, deep and muscular to support the massive head. The second vertebra, the axis, was especially short. The remaining neck vertebrae were weakly opisthocoelous, i.e. with a convex front of the vertebral body and a concave rear. The vertebral bodies had single pleurocoels, pneumatic depressions created by [air sacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_sac "Air sac"), on their sides.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10) The vertebral bodies of the torso were robust but with a narrow waist. Their undersides were keeled. The front sides were concave with a deep vertical trough. They had large pleurocoels. Their neural spines had very rough front and rear sides for the attachment of strong tendons. The sacral vertebrae were fused to each other, both in their vertebral bodies and neural spines. They were pneumatized. They were connected to the pelvis by transverse processes and sacral ribs. The tail was heavy and moderately long, in order to balance the massive head and torso and to provide space for massive [locomotor muscles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_locomotion "Animal locomotion") that attached to the thighbones. The thirteenth tail vertebra formed the transition point between the deep tail base and the middle tail that was stiffened by a rather long front articulation processes. The underside of the trunk was covered by eighteen or nineteen pairs of segmen... [truncated]

414|The [shoulder girdle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoulder_girdle "Shoulder girdle") was longer than the entire forelimb. The shoulder blade had a narrow shaft but was exceptionally expanded at its upper end. It connected via a long forward protrusion to the [coracoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coracoid "Coracoid"), which was rounded. Both shoulder blades were connected by a small [furcula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Furcula "Furcula"). The paired breast bones possibly were made of [cartilage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartilage "Cartilage") only.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)
415|
416|The forelimb or arm was very short. The upper arm bone, the humerus, was short but robust. It had a narrow upper end with an exceptionally rounded head. The lower arm bones, the [ulna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulna "Ulna") and radius, were straight elements, much shorter than the humerus. The second [metacarpal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacarpus "Metacarpus") was longer and wider than the first, whereas normally in theropods the opposite is true. The forelimbs had only two clawed fingers,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10) along with an additional splint-like small third [metacarpal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacarpus "Metacarpus") representing the remnant of a third digit.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-CLKC08-60)

419|
420|Pelvic girdle of specimen MOR 555

422|The [pelvis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelvis "Pelvis") was a large structure. Its upper bone, the [ilium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilium_(bone) "Ilium (bone)"), was both very long and high, providing an extensive attachment area for hindlimb muscles. The front [pubic bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pubic_bone "Pubic bone") ended in an enormous pubic boot, longer than the entire shaft of the element. The rear [ischium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ischium "Ischium") was slender and straight, pointing obliquely to behind and below.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)
423|
424|In contrast to the arms, the hindlimbs were among the longest in proportion to body size of any theropod. In the foot, the [metatarsus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metatarsus "Metatarsus") was "arctometatarsalian", meaning that the part of the third metatarsal near the ankle was pinched. The third metatarsal was also exceptionally sinuous.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10) Compensating for the immense bulk of the animal, many bones throughout the skeleton were hollowed, reducing its weight without significant loss of strength.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)

432|_Tyrannosaurus_ is the [type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_(biology) "Type (biology)") genus of the superfamily [Tyrannosauroidea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosauroidea "Tyrannosauroidea"), the [family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_(taxonomy) "Family (taxonomy)")[Tyrannosauridae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosauridae "Tyrannosauridae"), and the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae; in other words it is the standard by which paleontologists decide whether to include other species in the same group. Other members of the tyrannosaurine subfamily include the North American _[Daspletosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daspletosaurus "Daspletosaurus")_ and the Asian _[Tarbosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarbosaurus "Tarbosaurus")_,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-currieetal2003-25)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-holtz2004-61) both of which have occasionally been synonymized with _Tyrannosaurus_.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-paul1988-62)
433|
434|Tyrannosaurids were once commonly thought to be descendants of earlier large theropods such as [megalosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinosauroidea "Spinosauroidea") and [carnosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnosauria "Carnosauria"), although more recently they were reclassified with the generally smaller [coelurosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coelurosauria "Coelurosauria").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-holtz1994-51) The earliest tyrannosaur group were the crested proceratosaurids, while later and more derived members belong to the [Pantyrannosauria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantyrannosauria "Pantyrannosauria"). Tyrannosaurs started out as small theropods; however at least some became larger by the [Early Cretaceous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Cretaceous "Early Cretaceous"). It is quite likely that tyrannosauroids rose to prominence after the decline in allosauroid and megalosauroid diversity seen during the early stages of the Late Cretaceous.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-63)
435|
436|Tyrannosauroids are characterized by their fused nasals and dental arrangement. Pantyrannosaurs are characterized by unique features in their hips as well as an enlarged foramen in the quadrate, a broad postorbital and hourglass shaped nasals. Some of the more derived pantyrannosaurs lack nasal pneumaticity and have a lower humerus to femur ratio with their arms starting to see some reduction. Some pantyrannosaurs started developing an arctometatarsus. Eutyrannosaurs have a rough texture on their nasal bones and their mandibular fenestra is reduced externally. Tyrannosaurids lack kinetic skulls or special crests on their nasal bones, and have a lacrimal with a distinctive process on it. Tyrannosaurids also have an interfenestral strut that is less than half as big as the maxillary fenestra.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-64)
437|
438|Many [phylogenetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phylogeny "Phylogeny") analyses have found _[Tarbosaurus bataar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarbosaurus\_bataar "Tarbosaurus bataar")_ to be the [sister taxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sister_taxon "Sister taxon") of _T. rex_.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-holtz2004-61) The discovery of the tyrannosaurid _[Lythronax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lythronax "Lythronax")_ further indicates that _Tarbosaurus_ and _Tyrannosaurus_ are closely related, forming a clade with fellow Asian tyrannosaurid _[Zhuchengtyrannus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhuchengtyrannus "Zhuchengtyrannus")_, with _Lythronax_ being their sister taxon.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Loewen13-65)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-66) A further study from 2016 by Steve Brusatte, Thomas Carr and colleagues, also indicates that _Tyrannosaurus_ may have been an immigrant from Asia, as well as a possible descendant of _Tarbosaurus_.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-67)

454|In 1955, Soviet [paleontologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleontology "Paleontology")[Evgeny Maleev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evgeny_Maleev "Evgeny Maleev") named a new species, _Tyrannosaurus bataar_, from [Mongolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolia "Mongolia").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-maleev1955-70) By 1965, this species was renamed as a distinct genus, _Tarbosaurus bataar_.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-rozhdestvensky1965-71) While most paleontologists continue to maintain the two as distinct genera, some authors such as [Thomas Holtz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Holtz "Thomas Holtz"), [Kenneth Carpenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carpenter "Kenneth Carpenter"), and [Thomas Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Carr_(paleontologist) "Thomas Carr (paleontologist)") argue that the two species are similar enough to be considered members of the same genus, restoring the Mongolian [taxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxon "Taxon")'s original [binomial name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_nomenclature "Binomial nomenclature").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-holtz1994-51)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carpenter1992-72)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carr2017-55)
455|
456|Some specimens from the Late Cretaceous deposits of [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") have been described as new species of _Tyrannosaurus_: _T._ "lanpingensis" based on isolated [lateral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lateral_(anatomy) "Lateral (anatomy)") tooth from the red beds of [Yunnan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yunnan "Yunnan") in 1975; _T._ "turpanensis" from the [Subashi Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subashi_Formation "Subashi Formation"), [Turpan Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turpan_Basin "Turpan Basin"), [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang") in 1978; and _T. luanchuanensis_ from the [Quiba Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiba_Formation "Quiba Formation"), [Tantou Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tantou_Basin?action=edit&redlink=1 "Tantou Basin (page does not exist)"), [Henan Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henan_Province "Henan Province") in 1979–1980.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-73)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Feng2016-74)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Lucas2018-75) The former two taxa were published without detailed descriptions and are therefore nomina nuda. _T._ "turpanensis" and _T. luanchuanensis_ were tentatively listed as [junior synonyms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synonym_(taxonomy) "Synonym (taxonomy)") of _Tarbosaurus bataar_ by Holtz in 2004; Holtz also listed _T._ "lanpingensis," but as a nomen dubium.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-holtz2004-61)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Feng2016-74)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Lucas2018-75)
457|
458|VGI, no. 231/3, a large [phalanx bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phalanx_bone "Phalanx bone"), assigned to _Tyrannosaurus_ sp. by Yarkov in 2000, was found in the Lower Maastrichtian of [Bereslavka, Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bereslavka,_Russia "Bereslavka, Russia"). In 2004, Averianov and Yarkov reinterpreted it as a [metacarpal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacarpal "Metacarpal") I or [metatarsal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metatarsal "Metatarsal") I that possibly belongs to [ceratosaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceratosaur "Ceratosaur").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-76) In their 2023 overview, Averianov and Lopatin mention this specimen as well as a single tooth from the same site only as Theropoda indet.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-77)
459|
460|In 2001, various tyrannosaurid teeth and a metatarsal unearthed in a quarry near [Zhucheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhucheng "Zhucheng"), China, were assigned by Chinese paleontologist [Hu Chengzhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hu_Chengzhi "Hu Chengzhi") to the newly erected species _Tyrannosaurus zhuchengensis_. However, in a nearby site, a right maxilla and left jawbone were assigned to the newly erected tyrannosaurid genus _Zhuchengtyrannus_ in 2011. It is possible that _T. zhuchengensis_ is [synonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synonym_(taxonomy) "Synonym (taxonomy)") with _Zhuchengtyrannus_. In any case, _T. zhuchengensis_ is considered to be a _[nomen dubium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomen\_dubium "Nomen dubium")_ as the holotype lacks [diagnostic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagnosis_(taxonomy) "Diagnosis (taxonomy)") features below the level Tyrannosaurinae.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-78)
461|
462|In 2006, a fragmentary tyrannosaurid lacrimal (CM 9401) from the [Judith River Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_River_Formation "Judith River Formation") of Fergus County, Montana, was described as?_Tyrannosaurus_ sp. This isolated right lacrimal was originally collected alongside the holotype specimen of _Deinosuchus rugosus_, a giant crocodilian, and remained undescribed until its re-identification as belonging to a tyrannosaurid theropod in the 1980s by paleontologist [Dale Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dale_Russell "Dale Russell"). The lacrimal closely resembles those of _Tyrannosaurus rex_ in both size and morphology. Notably, it lacks the "lacrimal horn" typically present in earlier tyrannosaurids like _[Albertosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albertosaurus "Albertosaurus")_ and _[Gorgosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorgosaurus "Gorgosaurus")_, instead exhibiting a distinct rugosity along the dorsal surface—consistent with _T. rex_ and its Asian relative _Tarbosaurus_. The specimen's considerable size places it within the range of known _T. rex_ individuals, suggesting the presence of large tyrannosaurids during the Campanian stage (~75 million years ago), a temporal range earlier than the established Maastrichtian age (~68–66 Ma) for _Tyrannosaurus rex_. However, the exact age and provenance of CM 9401 remain uncertain due to a lack of detailed field documentation.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-79)
463|
464|In 2018, a paper describing tyrannosaurid teeth from the Two Medicine Formation noted a premaxillary tooth (YPM VPPU 023469) had a strong resemblance to the teeth of [Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(Tyrannosaurus) "Sue (Tyrannosaurus)") to the exclusion of any Campanian tyrannosaurid. Additionally, the authors of this paper suggested that CM 9401 also comes from the Two Medicine Formation, as there were preservational similarities between its locality and the Willow Creek anticline, which is where the tooth was found.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-80) Notably, this would place both specimens in the Flag Butte Member of the Two Medicine Formation, which dates from 77 to 76.3 Ma, far older than any other _Tyrannosaurus_ specimen, and directly contemporaneous with _Daspletosaurus._ In 2025, these specimens, with their old geologic age, were used as evidence by Charlie Scherer to suggest that the Tyrannosaurini did not evolve directly from _Daspletosaurus_.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Scherer2025-81)
465|
466|### _Tyrannosaurus imperator_ and _Tyrannosaurus regina_
467|
468|In a 2022 study, [Gregory S. Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_S._Paul "Gregory S. Paul") and colleagues argued that _Tyrannosaurus rex_, as traditionally understood, actually represents three species: the type species _Tyrannosaurus rex_, and two previously unrecognized species: _T. imperator_ (meaning "tyrant lizard emperor") and _T. regina_ (meaning "tyrant lizard queen"). The holotype of the former (_T. imperator_) is the [Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)") specimen, and the holotype of the latter (_T. regina_) is [Wankel rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wankel_rex "Wankel rex"). The division into multiple species was primarily based on the high degree of variation in the proportions and robusticity of the [femur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femur "Femur") (and other skeletal elements) across _T. rex_ specimens. Presumed robust and gracile morphotypes and the number of small incisiform teeth in the dentary were also used as a line of evidence. Paul and colleagues categorized the species as follows: _T. rex_ demonstrates robust anatomy, a moderate ratio of femur length vs circumference, and the possession of a singular slender incisiform dentary tooth, _T. imperator_ is robust with a small femur length to circumference ratio and two of the slender teeth, and _T. regina_ is more gracile with a high femur ratio and one of the slender teeth.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-paul2022-82)
469|
470|However, several leading paleontologists, including [Stephen Brusatte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Brusatte "Stephen Brusatte"), [Thomas Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Carr_(paleontologist) "Thomas Carr (paleontologist)"), [Thomas Holtz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Holtz "Thomas Holtz"), David Hone, [Jingmai O'Connor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingmai_O'Connor "Jingmai O'Connor"), and [Lindsay Zanno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindsay_Zanno "Lindsay Zanno"), criticized the study or expressed skepticism of its conclusions when approached by various media outlets for comment.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-newyorktimes-83)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-84)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-85) Their criticism was subsequently published in a technical paper.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Carr_et.al.(2022)-86) Holtz and Zanno both remarked that it was plausible that more than one species of _Tyrannosaurus_ existed, but felt the new study was insufficient to support the species it proposed. Holtz remarked that, even if _Tyrannosaurus imperator_ represented a distinct species from _Tyrannosaurus rex_, it may represent the same species as _Nanotyrannus lancensis_ and would need to be called _Tyrannosaurus lancensis_. O'Connor, a curator at the Field Museum, where the _T. imperator_ holotype Sue is displayed, regarded the new species as too poorly-supported to justify modifying the exhibit signs. Brusatte, Carr, and O'Connor viewed the distinguishing features proposed between the species as reflecting natural variation within a species. Both Carr and O'Connor expressed concerns about the study's inability to determine which of the proposed species several well-preserved specimens belonged to. Another paleontologist, [Philip J. Currie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_J._Currie "Philip J. Currie"), originally co-authored... [truncated]
471|
472|In a subsequent paper published in 2025, Paul maintained the validity of _T. imperator_ and _T. regina_, arguing that these proposed species could be further distinguished by the shape of their postorbital bosses (bony rugosities behind the eyes).[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Paul2025-87)

474|### _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_
475|
476|[![Image 43](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis_%28skull_reconstruction%29.png/250px-Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis_%28skull_reconstruction%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis_(skull_reconstruction).png)

479|
480|Reconstructed skull (top) and speculative [life restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_restoration "Life restoration") (bottom) of _T. mcraeensis_
481|
482|In 2024, Dalman and colleagues [described](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species_description "Species description") the remains of a tyrannosaur discovered in 1983 in the Campanian-early Maastrichtian [Hall Lake Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall_Lake_Formation "Hall Lake Formation") in New Mexico. Reposited at the [New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Science "New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science"), the fossil material (NMMNH P-3698) consists of the right [postorbital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postorbital "Postorbital"), right [squamosal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squamosal "Squamosal"), left [palatine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palatine "Palatine"), and an incomplete [maxilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxilla "Maxilla") from the skull, the left [dentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dentary "Dentary"), right [splenial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splenial "Splenial"), right prearticular, right [angular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_bone "Angular bone") and right [articular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articular "Articular") from the lower jaws, isolated teeth, and [chevrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haemal_arch "Haemal arch").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-T.mcraeensis-68) Some of the bones were briefly mentioned in 1984 as belonging to _T. rex_,[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Lozinsky1984-88) and described in 1986.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Gillette1986-89)
483|
484|Lehman and Carpenter (1990) suggested that NMMNH P-3698 belonged to a new tyrannosaurid genus,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-90) while Carr and Williamson (2000) disagreed with their claim.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-91) Sullivan and Lucas (2015) argued that there is little evidence to support NMMNH P-3698 as a specimen of _Tyrannosaurus rex_, so they tentatively classified it as cf. _Tyrannosaurus_ sp.; they also considered that the McRae tyrannosaur lived before the [Lancian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancian "Lancian") (before 67 million years ago) based on its probable association with the _[Alamosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alamosaurus "Alamosaurus")_ fossil.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-92)
485|
486|[![Image 45](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis_%28mandibular_elements%29.png/250px-Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis_%28mandibular_elements%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis_(mandibular_elements).png)
487|
488|Mandibular elements of the _T. mcraeensis_ holotype
489|
490|Dalman et al. (2024) proposed the new name _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_ for the holotype (NMMNH P-3698), referencing the McRae Group, the rock layers to which the Hall Lake Formation belongs. The holotype of _T. mcraeensis_ is found in the strata that are around a few million years older than the accepted range of _T. rex_, which existed at the end of the Maastrichtian. The rock layers were initially estimated to date to between 72.7 and 70.9 Ma, correlating to the latest Campanian or earliest Maastrichtian.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-T.mcraeensis-68) However, in a 2024 conference [abstract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_(summary) "Abstract (summary)"), the specific stratigraphic layer which yielded _T. mcraeensis_ was estimated to be younger than 69.0 ± 0.4 Ma and older than 66.0 Ma based on the sandstone from the same fossil locality,[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-93) which would suggest that the age of _T. mcraeensis_ is much closer to _T. rex_ than previously thought.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Scherer2025-81)_T. mcraeensis_ was estimated at 12 metres (39 ft) long, which is similar to the size of an adult _T. rex_. The two are distinguished by characters of the skull. Amongst these, the dentary of _T. mcraeensis_ is proportionately longer and possesses a less prominent chin, and the lower jaw shallower than that of _T. rex_, suggesting a weaker bite. The teeth are likewise blunter and more laterally compressed, while the post orbital crests are less prominent. Likewise, the skeletal anatomy showcases shared characteristics with _Tarbosaurus_ and _Zhuchengtyrannus_.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-T.mcraeensis-68)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-NYT-20240111-94)
491|
492|The validity of _T. mcraeensis_ was subsequently questioned by other researchers in 2025. Morrison and colleagues noted the uncertainty in the previous age estimate of _T. mcraeensis_. The authors argued that the inclusion of the titanosaurian fossil (cf. _Alamosaurus_) as a biostratigraphic marker of the Hall Lake Formation fauna makes the dating problematic due to the fossil having a huge variability in assumed sedimentation rates. The study also suggested the uncertainty in the morphology of _T. mcraeensis_ holotype being reliably outside the known variation of _T. rex_. Regardless of the age and validity of _T. mcraeensis_, the authors concluded that the genus _Tyrannosaurus_ still most likely originated from Laramidia and that the ancestors of this genus possibly migrated from Asia.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-95) Later that year, Voris and colleagues regarded _T. mcraeensis_ as a [junior synonym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_synonym "Junior synonym") of _T. rex_, agreeing with the problematic stratigraphic data and finding all of the proposed diagnostic characters of _T. mcraeensis_ to be in the known _T. rex_ specimen range of variation.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-voris25-96) In his study of the _T. rex_ holotype skull, Carr also did not regard _T. mcraeensis_ as a valid species, agreeing with the proposed characters of the _T. mcraeensis_ holotype being visible throughout the hypodigm of _T. rex_.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-97)

502|Other tyrannosaur fossils found in the same formations as _T. rex_ were originally classified as separate taxa, including _Aublysodon_ and _Albertosaurus megagracilis_,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-paul1988-62) the latter being named _Dinotyrannus megagracilis_ in 1995.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Olshevsky1995-98) These fossils are now universally considered to belong to juvenile _T. rex_.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carrwilliamson2004-99) A small but nearly complete skull from Montana, 57.2 centimeters (1.88 ft) long, is an exception. This skull, [CMNH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Museum_of_Natural_History "Cleveland Museum of Natural History") 7541, was originally classified as a species of _[Gorgosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorgosaurus "Gorgosaurus")_ (_G. lancensis_) by [Charles W. Gilmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_W._Gilmore "Charles W. Gilmore") in 1946.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-gilmore1946-100) In 1988, the specimen was re-described by [Robert T. Bakker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_T._Bakker "Robert T. Bakker"), Michael Williams, then the curator of paleontology at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History, and [Phil Currie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_J._Currie "Philip J. Currie"), where the original specimen was housed and is now on display. Their initial research indicated that the skull bones were fused, and that it therefore represented an adult specimen. In light of this, Bakker and colleagues assigned the skull to a new genus named _Nanotyrannus_ (meaning "dwarf tyrant", for its apparently small adult size).[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-bakkeretal1988-101) However, in 1999, a detailed analysis by [Thomas Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Carr_(paleontologist) "Thomas Carr (paleontologist)") revealed the specimen to be a juvenile, lea... [truncated]

508|In 2001, a more complete juvenile tyrannosaur (nicknamed "Jane", [accession number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accession_number_(cultural_property) "Accession number (cultural property)") BMRP 2002.4.1), suggested to belong to the same species as the original _Nanotyrannus_ specimen, was uncovered. This discovery prompted a conference on tyrannosaurs focused on the issues of the validity of _Nanotyrannus_, held at the [Burpee Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burpee_Museum_of_Natural_History "Burpee Museum of Natural History") in 2005. Several paleontologists who had previously published opinions that _N. lancensis_ was a valid species, including Currie and Williams, saw the discovery of "Jane" as a confirmation that _Nanotyrannus_ was, in fact, a juvenile _T. rex_.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-currie2003a-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-currieetal2005-105)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-henderson2005-106)[Peter Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Larson "Peter Larson") continued to support the hypothesis that _Nanotyrannus lancensis_ was a separate but closely related species, and also argued that _[Stygivenator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stygivenator "Stygivenator")_ (LACM 28471), which is generally considered to be a juvenile of _Tyrannosaurus rex_, could be a younger specimen of _Nanotyrannus_.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-larson13-107)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-108)
509|
510|In late 2011, news reports about a 2006 discovery of a new, virtually complete theropod specimen found alongside a [ceratopsid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceratopsid "Ceratopsid") were made. The specimens were studied by Robert Bakker and Peter Larson on-site, who identified the ceratopsian as _[Triceratops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triceratops "Triceratops")_ and the theropod as _Nanotyrannus_.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Nano_Smithsonian_2011-109) It was impossible to determine whether the theropod specimen, nicknamed "Bloody Mary", was distinct from _T. rex_, as the specimen remained in private hands until 2020, when the ownership of the specimen was decided by the [Montana Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana_Supreme_Court "Montana Supreme Court") to be given to the landowners Mary Anne and Lige Murray, who agreed to sell the paired fossils to a U.S.-based museum.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-110) The fossil was acquired by the [North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_Museum_of_Natural_Sciences "North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences") in 2020, after which the museum built an additional research lab space in which to [prepare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil_preparation "Fossil preparation"), study, and display the specimens.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-111)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-112) In 2025, paleontologists [Lindsay Zanno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindsay_Zanno "Lindsay Zanno") and James Napoli published an initial description of the "Bloody Mary" specimen as part of an extensive revision of the genus _Nanotyrannus_. They identified this specimen as a skeletally mature individual of _Nanotyrannus_ and provided several lines of evidence supporting the validity of this genus. They also described a second species, _N. lethaeus_, based on the Jan... [truncated]

512|## Paleobiology
513|
514|### Life history
515|
516|[![Image 48](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Juvenile_Tyrannosaurus_skull_LACM.jpg/250px-Juvenile_Tyrannosaurus_skull_LACM.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Juvenile_Tyrannosaurus_skull_LACM.jpg)
517|
518|Skull of a juvenile _T. rex_ formerly classified as _Dinotyrannus megagracilis_
519|
520|The identification of several specimens as juvenile _T. rex_ has allowed scientists to document [ontogenetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontogeny "Ontogeny") changes in the species, estimate the lifespan, and determine how quickly the animals would have grown. The _Stygivenator_ holotype ([LACM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County_Museum_of_Natural_History "Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History") 28471, the "Jordan theropod"), possibly a juvenile _T. rex_, is estimated to have weighed only 30 kg (66 lb), while the largest adults, such as [FMNH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") PR2081 (Sue) most likely weighed about 5,650 kg (12,460 lb). [Histologic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histology "Histology") analysis of _T. rex_ bones showed LACM 28471 had aged only 2 years when it died. Sue was initially estimated at 28 years old, an age which was at the time considered close to the maximum for the species,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-ericksonetal2004-41) but the most recent studies estimate Sue's age at 27–33 years.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-113) Similarly, [Trix (RGM 792.000)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trix_(dinosaur) "Trix (dinosaur)") is estimated to have been at least 30 years old at time of death.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-114)
521|
522|Histology has also allowed the age of other specimens to be determined. Growth curves can be developed when the ages of different specimens are plotted on a graph along with their mass. A _T. rex_ growth curve is S-shaped, with juveniles remaining under 1,800 kg (4,000 lb) until approximately 14 years of age, when body size began to increase dramatically. During this rapid growth phase, a young _T. rex_ would gain an average of 600 kg (1,300 lb) a year for the next four years. At 18 years of age, the curve plateaus again, indicating that growth slowed dramatically. For example, only 600 kg (1,300 lb) separated the 28-year-old Sue from a 22-year-old Canadian specimen ([RTMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Tyrrell_Museum_of_Palaeontology "Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology") 81.12.1).[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-ericksonetal2004-41) A 2004 histological study performed by different workers corroborates these results, finding that rapid growth began to slow at around 16 years of age.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-hornerpadian2004-115)
523|
524|[![Image 49](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Tyrannosauridae_growth_rates.svg/250px-Tyrannosauridae_growth_rates.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosauridae_growth_rates.svg)
525|
526|A graph showing the hypothesized growth curve, body mass versus age (drawn in black, with other tyrannosaurids for comparison), based on Erickson and colleagues 2004. Studies like this are now known to have been skewed by the inclusion of specimens now considered _Nanotyrannus_
527|
528|A study by Hutchinson and colleagues in 2011 corroborated the previous estimation methods in general, but their estimation of peak growth rates is significantly higher; it found that the "maximum growth rates for T. rex during the exponential stage are 1790 kg/year".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Hutchinsonet.al.2011-30) Although these results were much higher than previous estimations, the authors noted that these results significantly lowered the great difference between its actual growth rate and the one which would be expected of an animal of its size.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Hutchinsonet.al.2011-30) The sudden change in growth rate at the end of the growth spurt may indicate physical maturity, a hypothesis which is supported by the discovery of medullary tissue in the [femur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femur "Femur") of a 16 to 20-year-old _T. rex_ from Montana ([MOR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_the_Rockies "Museum of the Rockies") 1125, also known as [B-rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-rex "B-rex")). Medullary tissue is found only in female birds during ovulation, indicating that B-rex was of reproductive age.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-schweitzeretal2005-116) Further study indicates an age of 18 for this specimen.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-LW08-117) In 2016, it was finally confirmed by Mary Higby Schweitzer and Lindsay Zanno and colleagues that the soft tissue within the femur of MOR 1125 was medullary tissue. This also confirmed the identity of the specimen as a female. The discovery of [medullary bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medullary_bone "Medullary bone") tissue within _Tyrannosaurus_ may prove valuable in determining the sex of other dinosaur species in future examinations, as the chemical makeup of medullary tissue is unmistakable.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-118... [truncated]
529|
530|An additional study published in 2020 by Woodward and colleagues, for the journal _Science Advances_ indicates that during their growth from juvenile to adult, _Tyrannosaurus_ was capable of slowing down its growth to counter environmental factors such as lack of food. Based on BMRP 2002.4.1 and BMRP 2006.4.4 between 13 and 15 years old housed at the Burpee Museum in Illinois then referred to as juvenile _Tyrannosaurus_ specimens, the authors suggested that the rate of maturation for _Tyrannosaurus_ was dependent on resource abundance. This study also indicates that in such changing environments, _Tyrannosaurus_ was particularly well-suited to an environment that shifted yearly in regards to resource abundance, hinting that other midsize predators might have had difficulty surviving in such harsh conditions and explaining the niche partitioning between juvenile and adult tyrannosaurs. The study further suggested that _Tyrannosaurus_ and _Nanotyrannus_ are synonymous, due to analysis of the growth rings in the bones of the two specimens studied.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-120)[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-121)
531|
532|In January 2026, Woodward, Myhrvold and Horner performed a comprehensive histological analysis of 17 tyrannosaur specimens, and argued that _Tyrannosaurus_ likely experienced a more gradual annual growth rate slope than indicated by earlier studies and evidence of a protracted subadult stage, reaching asymptotic size at around 35–40 years of age. The upper limit of the annual growth rate estimate is approximately 43–53 years. They also found that the growth trajectories of BMRP 2002.4.1 and BMRP 2006.4.4 do not fit with other _Tyrannosaurus_ specimens in their growth curve model. While they acknowledged the possibility of these ontogenetically immature specimens representing _Nanotyrannus_ as suggested by Zanno and Napoli (2025), they noted that the inconsistencies of these specimens observed in the growth curve do not necessarily bear weight on the proposal that _Nanotyrannus_ is a distinct taxon.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-122)
533|
534|In July 2026, Longrich and colleagues described a third metatarsal bone of perinate (hatchling) _Tyrannosaurus rex_ and cf. _Gorgosaurus libratus_, RSKM P2416.82 from the [Frenchman Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frenchman_Formation "Frenchman Formation") and TMP 1981.16.475 from the [Dinosaur Park Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur_Park_Formation "Dinosaur Park Formation") respectively. Histological analyses reveal that lines of arrested growth are absent in both specimens, indicative of hatchling or embryonic stage. Synchrotron scans of each specimen reveal the relatively high density of the outer surface and the pattern changes in cortical (outer layer) bone structure, with a layer similar to the hatchling/[neonatal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neonate "Neonate") line of modern oviparous (egg-laying) and viviparous (giving live birth) taxa that characterize the transition from embryonic to hatchling stage. The scans also detected evidence of Haversian bone remodeling, the continuous process of bone tissue breaking down and rebuilding to form secondary canals (tubular channels connecting bones), which are indicative of hatchling stage and [precociality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precociality "Precociality"), relative maturity and mobility at birth. The layer lining the [medullary cavity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medullary_cavity "Medullary cavity") of both specimens likely represent endosteal bone deposition, during which new bone matrix is deposited on the inner surface of the cortical bone. The authors also described a partial dentary (FMNH PR 4920) from the Hell Creek Formation and isolated teeth from the Lance Formation as hatchling _T. rex_ and interpret their tooth wear as evidence of consuming relatively large vertebrates.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Longrich2026-123)
535|
536|The body length and body mass of the hatchling _T. rex_ (RSKM P2416.82) are estimated to be approximately 75 cm (2.46 ft) and 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) respectively, and those of the hatchling cf. _G. libratus_ (TMP 1981.16.475) are estimated to be approximately 70 cm (2.3 ft) and 2.4 kg (5.3 lb) respectively. On the basis of these body size estimates, Longrich et al. (2026) suggested that the clutch of the confirmed, reproductively mature female _T. rex_ (MOR 1125) would have weighed at least 54–60 kg (119–132 lb) which would possibly correspond to 21-32 eggs. They further stated that larger clutch sizes are also plausible, indicating that tyrannosaurids possibly employed [R-selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R-selection "R-selection"), a reproductive strategy that maximizes the number of offsprings through large clutch size and minimal parental investment, which would have resulted in rapid maturation of the hatchlings, slower than that of modern birds. It is also likely that the reproduction strategy of tyrannosaurids was an intermediate between R-selection and [K-selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-selection "K-selection"), the latter of which would maximize parental investment with fewer number of offsprings and delayed maturation. Given the uniparental care observed in modern crocodilians and basal (early-diverging) birds, most non-avian dinosaurs including _T. rex_ were likely uniparental as well. The authors also estimated that the relative size of tyrannosaurid hatchlings and eggs are larger than that of squamates, turtles, crocodilians, pterosaurs, and certain dinosaur clades (protoceratopsids and basal sauropodomorphs), but smaller than that of eumaniraptorans and modern birds, probably weighing less in both relative and absolute size than those of the [elephant bird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elephant_bird "Elephant bird")_[Aepyornis maximus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aepyornis\_maximus "Aepyornis maximus")_ and the [South Island giant moa](ht... [truncated]
537|
538|Over half of the known _T. rex_ specimens appear to have died within six years of reaching sexual maturity, a pattern which is also seen in other tyrannosaurs and in some large, long-lived birds and mammals today. These species are characterized by high infant mortality rates, followed by relatively low mortality among juveniles. Mortality increases again following sexual maturity, partly due to the stresses of reproduction. One study suggests that the rarity of juvenile _T. rex_ fossils is due in part to low juvenile mortality rates; the animals were not dying in large numbers at these ages, and thus were not often fossilized. This rarity may also be due to the incompleteness of the [fossil record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil_record "Fossil record") or to the bias of fossil collectors towards larger, more spectacular specimens.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-ericksonetal2006-119) In a 2013 lecture, Thomas Holtz Jr. suggested that dinosaurs "lived fast and died young" because they reproduced quickly whereas mammals have long lifespans because they take longer to reproduce.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-HoltzLecture2013-124) Gregory S. Paul also writes that _Tyrannosaurus_ reproduced quickly and died young but attributes their short lifespans to the dangerous lives they lived.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Paul2008Highrisklife-125)

548|The discovery of [feathered dinosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feathered_dinosaur "Feathered dinosaur") led to debate regarding whether, and to what extent, _Tyrannosaurus_ might have been feathered.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Belletal2017-126)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-NYT-20190307-127) Filamentous structures, which are commonly recognized as the precursors of [feathers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feather "Feather"), have been reported in the small-bodied, basal tyrannosauroid _[Dilong paradoxus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilong\_paradoxus "Dilong paradoxus")_ from the Early Cretaceous [Yixian Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yixian_Formation "Yixian Formation") of China in 2004.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-xuetal2004-128) Because [integumentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integument "Integument") impressions of larger tyrannosauroids known at that time showed evidence of [scales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scale_(anatomy) "Scale (anatomy)"), the researchers who studied _Dilong_ speculated that insulating feathers might have been lost by larger species due to their smaller surface-to-volume ratio.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-xuetal2004-128) The subsequent discovery of the giant species _[Yutyrannus huali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yutyrannus\_huali "Yutyrannus huali")_, also from the Yixian, showed that even some large tyrannosauroids had feathers covering much of their bodies, casting doubt on the hypothesis that they were a size-related feature.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-yutyrannus-129) A 2017 study reviewed known skin impressions of tyrannosaurids, including those of a _Tyrannosaurus_ specimen nicknamed "Wyrex" (HMNS 2006.1743.01, formerly known as BHI 6230) which preserves patches of mosaic scales on the tail, hip, and neck.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ty... [truncated]
549|
550|A conference abstract published in 2016 posited that theropods such as _Tyrannosaurus_ had their upper teeth covered in lips, instead of bare teeth as seen in [crocodilians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodilia "Crocodilia"). This was based on the presence of [enamel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tooth_enamel "Tooth enamel"), which according to the study needs to remain hydrated, an issue not faced by aquatic animals like crocodilians.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-:0-57) However, there has been criticism where it favors the idea for lips, with the 2017 analytical study proposing that tyrannosaurids had large, flat scales on their snouts instead of lips, as modern crocodiles do.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carr2017-55)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-naish2018-130) But crocodiles possess rather cracked keratinized skin, not flat scales; by observing the hummocky rugosity of tyrannosaurids, and comparing it to extant lizards, researchers have found that tyrannosaurids had squamose scales rather than a crocodillian-like skin.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-MontevialeCroc-58)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-131)
551|
552|In 2023, Cullen and colleagues supported the idea that theropods like tyrannosaurids had lips based on anatomical patterns, such as those of the foramina on their face and jaws, more similar to those of modern [squamates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squamate "Squamate") such as [monitor lizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monitor_lizard "Monitor lizard") or [marine iguanas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_iguana "Marine iguana") than those of modern [crocodilians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodilia "Crocodilia") like [alligators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alligator "Alligator"). Comparison of the teeth of _Daspletosaurus_ and [American alligators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_alligator "American alligator") shows that the enamel of tyrannosaurids had no significant wear and that the teeth of modern crocodilians were eroded on the labial side and were substantially worn. This suggests that it is likely that theropod teeth were kept wet by lips. On the basis of the relationship between hydration and wear resistance, the authors argued that it is unlikely that the teeth of theropods, including tyrannosaurids, would have remained unworn when exposed for a long time, because it would have been hard to maintain hydration. The authors also performed regression analyses to demonstrate the relationship between tooth height and skull length, and found that [varanids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varanid "Varanid") like the [crocodile monitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodile_monitor "Crocodile monitor") had substantially greater ratios of tooth height to skull length than those of _Tyrannosaurus_, indicating that the teeth of theropods were not too big to be covered by extraoral tissues when the mouth was closed.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-CullenEtAl23-59)

555|
556|[![Image 51](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/MUJA_04.jpg/250px-MUJA_04.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MUJA_04.jpg)

558|Skeleton casts mounted in a mating position, [Jurassic Museum of Asturias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurassic_Museum_of_Asturias "Jurassic Museum of Asturias")
559|
560|As the number of known specimens increased, scientists began to analyze the variation between individuals and discovered what appeared to be two distinct body types, or _morphs_, similar to some other theropod species. As one of these morphs was more solidly built, it was termed the 'robust' morph while the other was termed '[gracile](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/gracile "wikt:gracile")'. Several [morphological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morphology_(biology) "Morphology (biology)") differences associated with the two morphs were used to analyze [sexual dimorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_dimorphism "Sexual dimorphism") in _T. rex_, with the 'robust' morph usually suggested to be female. For example, the [pelvis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelvis "Pelvis") of several 'robust' specimens seemed to be wider, perhaps to allow the passage of [eggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egg_(biology) "Egg (biology)").[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carpenter1990-132) It was also thought that the 'robust' morphology correlated with a reduced [chevron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevron_(anatomy) "Chevron (anatomy)") on the first tail vertebra, also ostensibly to allow eggs to pass out of the [reproductive tract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reproductive_system "Reproductive system"), as had been erroneously reported for [crocodiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodile "Crocodile").[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-larson1994-133)
561|
562|In recent years, evidence for sexual dimorphism has been weakened. A 2005 study reported that previous claims of sexual dimorphism in crocodile chevron anatomy were in error, casting doubt on the existence of similar dimorphism between _T. rex_ sexes.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-ericksonetal2005-134) A full-sized chevron was discovered on the first tail vertebra of Sue, an extremely robust individual, indicating that this feature could not be used to differentiate the two morphs anyway. As _T. rex_ specimens have been found from [Saskatchewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskatchewan "Saskatchewan") to [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico"), differences between individuals may be indicative of geographic variation rather than sexual dimorphism. The differences could also be age-related, with 'robust' individuals being older animals.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)
563|
564|Only a single _Tyrannosaurus_ specimen has been conclusively shown to belong to a specific sex. Examination of B-rex demonstrated the preservation of [soft tissue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_tissue "Soft tissue") within several bones. Some of this tissue has been identified as a medullary tissue, a specialized tissue grown only in modern birds as a source of [calcium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium "Calcium") for the production of [eggshell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eggshell "Eggshell") during [ovulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovulation "Ovulation"). As only female birds lay eggs, medullary tissue is only found naturally in females, although males are capable of producing it when injected with female reproductive [hormones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hormone "Hormone") like [estrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estrogen "Estrogen"). This strongly suggests that B-rex was female and that she died during ovulation.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-schweitzeretal2005-116) Recent research has shown that medullary tissue is never found in [crocodilians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodilian "Crocodilian"), which are thought to be the closest living relatives of dinosaurs. The shared presence of medullary tissue in birds and other theropod dinosaurs is further evidence of the close [evolutionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolution "Evolution") relationship between the two.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-schweitzeretal2007-135)

568|[![Image 52](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/T._rex_old_posture.jpg/250px-T._rex_old_posture.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:T._rex_old_posture.jpg)

572|Like many [bipedal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipedal "Bipedal") dinosaurs, _T. rex_ was historically depicted as a 'living tripod', with the body at 45 degrees or less from the vertical and the tail dragging along the ground, similar to a [kangaroo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangaroo "Kangaroo"). This concept dates from [Joseph Leidy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Leidy "Joseph Leidy")'s 1865 reconstruction of _[Hadrosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrosaurus "Hadrosaurus")_, the first to depict a dinosaur in a bipedal posture.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-leidy1865-136) In 1915, convinced that the creature stood upright, [Henry Fairfield Osborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Fairfield_Osborn "Henry Fairfield Osborn"), former president of the American Museum of Natural History, further reinforced the notion in unveiling the first complete _T. rex_ skeleton arranged this way. It stood in an upright pose for 77 years, until it was dismantled in 1992.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-amnhsite-137)
573|
574|By 1970, scientists realized this pose was incorrect and could not have been maintained by a living animal, as it would have resulted in the [dislocation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dislocation_(medicine) "Dislocation (medicine)") or weakening of several [joints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint "Joint"), including the hips and the articulation between the head and the [spinal column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinal_column "Spinal column").[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-newman1970-138) The inaccurate AMNH mount inspired similar depictions in many films and paintings (such as [Rudolph Zallinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolph_F._Zallinger "Rudolph F. Zallinger")'s famous mural _[The Age of Reptiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Age\_of\_Reptiles "The Age of Reptiles")_ in [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University")'s [Peabody Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peabody_Museum_of_Natural_History "Peabody Museum of Natural History"))[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-139) until the 1990s, when films such as _[Jurassic Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurassic\_Park\_(film) "Jurassic Park (film)")_ introduced a more accurate posture to the general public.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-140) Modern representations in museums, art, and film show _T. rex_ with its body approximately parallel to the ground with the tail extended behind the body to balance the head.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-141)
575|
576|To sit down, _Tyrannosaurus_ may have settled its weight backwards and rested its weight on a pubic boot, the wide expansion at the end of the pubis in some dinosaurs. With its weight rested on the pelvis, it may have been free to move the hindlimbs. Getting back up again might have involved some stabilization from the diminutive forelimbs.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-142)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-newman1970-138) The latter known as Newman's pushup theory has been debated. Nonetheless, _Tyrannosaurus_ was probably able to get up if it fell, which only would have required placing the limbs below the center of gravity, with the tail as an effective counterbalance. Healed stress fractures in the forelimbs have been put forward both as evidence that the arms cannot have been very useful[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-143)[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Padian_(2022)-144) and as evidence that they were indeed used and acquired wounds,[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Stevens_et.al.2008-145) like the rest of the body.
